objects.argument:
The pre-admission GP record is the cleanest control source because it records the presentation before the hospital's later classification became the dominant organising frame.

The GP first documented bilateral foot pain and abnormal gait. The record then evolved: impaired initiation of movement; explicit consideration of Neurology for the patient's “gait, feet and 'muscle tension' issues”; Occupational Health concern; marked increased tone in both legs; worsening dexterity; inability to perform work; and direct neurological assessment.

That chronology does not prove one mechanism. It does establish that the patient arrived at hospital through a **single evolving neurological referral pathway** in which feet, gait, tone, movement initiation, dexterity and function were materially connected enough to require neurological investigation.

The July hospital record then preserves both sides of the presentation: genuine structural foot abnormalities and severe neurological findings, including a footdrop-like gait somewhat suggestive of dystonic posture. Crucially, the relationship is not recorded as resolved. It is recorded as **“Not clear”.**
objects.evidential_status:
**Document-only.** No later patient recollection is required.

---
objects.question: Was the hospital presented with two already-separated problems — Parkinsonism and unrelated feet — or with one evolving presentation whose internal relationships were still unresolved?
objects.strongest_alternative_explanation: The structural foot disease was independently real and could appropriately have been managed by Podiatry even while Neurology addressed Parkinsonism.
objects.surviving_point: That explanation supports parallel care, but it does not convert the unresolved relationship into a documented finding of neurological separateness.
objects.title: Stage One — What entered Neurology?

objects.argument:
The record shows a transition from **uncertainty at the level of explanation** to **definiteness at the level of management and administration**.

Neurology retained the Parkinsonian syndrome. Podiatry became the practical pathway for the feet. Parkinson's disease became an administrative category. A deliberate treatment-deferral policy was established.

The important documentary point is not that these actions were necessarily wrong. It is that they became operative **before the internal relationship within the original presentation had been resolved**.

The 6 July GP note sharpens this point. Podiatry was being asked to prioritise the case “as Parkinson's”. Therefore, the mere existence of a Podiatry pathway cannot later be treated as proof that the feet had already been clinically demonstrated to be unrelated to the neurological syndrome.

At the same time, the hospital record distinguished syndrome-level certainty from etiological certainty. Parkinsonism was sufficiently established for treatment and administration while subtype, genetics and the foot relationship remained open.

The record also expressly contains the treating neurologist's statement that he was not a movement-disorders neurologist. That does not establish lack of competence or authority. It does identify a documentary asymmetry: **claimed interpretive limitation coexisted with durable operative decision-making**.
objects.question: How did an expressly unresolved relationship become a definite operational arrangement?
objects.strongest_alternative_explanation: Clinical systems routinely make practical allocations before every causal question is resolved. Administrative coding can operate at syndrome level, and Podiatry can appropriately manage visible structural disease.
objects.surviving_point: Agreed. The issue is not whether operational action was permissible. The issue is that the later record should not retrospectively treat the operational allocation itself as proof that the original unresolved relationship had been clinically adjudicated.
objects.title: Stage Two — What happened to the unresolved presentation?

objects.argument:
The levodopa/dopamine-agonist deferral was not accidental or incidental. It was an articulated policy based on unusually young onset and concern about long-term treatment complications.

The same record expressly recognised the counterweight: dopamine replacement would probably become necessary; it might produce substantial benefit; and the team might later regret not having introduced it earlier.

That combination is important because the plan contains a recognised failure mode but the surviving record does not identify an equally explicit **escape condition** — a defined evidential, symptomatic or functional threshold that would require the strategy to be reconsidered.

A related pattern appears in the genetics reasoning. The record expressly asks what value a firm genetic diagnosis would have if it would not change management. By April 2018, the logic is stated more directly: there was “no great loss” in not knowing because the result would not particularly change current management.

Meanwhile, the PARK2/PRKN branch became increasingly specific. Prof Healy independently wrote that the patient probably had PARK II and proposed PARK II testing first. Galway later recorded PARK2/PRKN as the suspected cause.

The documentary concern is therefore not simply delay. It is the relationship between **management stability and information value**: the record shows diagnostic information being assessed partly by whether it would alter a plan already expected to remain substantially unchanged.
objects.evidential_status:
**Document-only for the existence and wording of the strategy.**  
**Expert evidence required** to determine whether the strategy was clinically appropriate.

---
objects.question: What did the July 2017 treatment strategy commit the case to, and what did the record say would cause that strategy to change?
objects.strongest_alternative_explanation: There may have been sound clinical reasons to defer both levodopa and genetic testing. Younger patients may face particular long-term treatment complications, and genetic confirmation may not change immediate symptomatic management.
objects.surviving_point: That explanation may justify the decisions clinically. It does not answer the documentary question of what evidence would reopen the strategy, or whether a management plan should also determine the value assigned to information capable of challenging its own assumptions.
objects.title: Stage Three — What management plan became durable?

objects.argument:
No single later event is sufficient to prove one historical mechanism. The force lies in the accumulation.

The record documents meaningful improvement on Procyclidine and deterioration when it was withdrawn. The withdrawal episode includes a lower-limb/foot-specific signal: the rapid return of the outside-left-foot phenomenon alongside worsening tension and movement.

In 2020, a treating neurologist expressly classified a foot-throw resembling foot drop as parkinsonian after documenting normal ankle power.

In 2021, ordinary levodopa treatment finally entered the case in a context of worsening aches, pains and stiffness. By December 2021, “re-emerging dystonia and altered gait” were expressly used as reasons to increase levodopa exposure.

In 2023, severe foot/leg pain, reduced mobility and shuffling were documented in relation to medication timing, and a clinician assessed the leg pain and shuffling as OFF-related. A morning Stalevo substitution was then structured as a trial to see whether symptoms improved.

By 2025, Sinemet CR was being used in part to address the morning experience including pain, and a later clinician account described profound relief after escalation while still preserving mixed or peripheral mechanisms.

The proper proposition is therefore not that all foot pathology was neurological. It is that **the longitudinal medication-state record repeatedly generated evidence capable of bearing on the original unresolved lower-limb/foot relationship**.
objects.evidential_status:
**Document-only for the existence of the later treatment-state evidence.**  
**Expert evidence required** for mechanism and causal allocation.

---
objects.question: Did later records produce information capable of testing or qualifying the original 2017 foot–neurology uncertainty?
objects.strongest_alternative_explanation: The later phenomena may not all be identical. Structural pathology, neuropathic pain, altered loading, dystonia, OFF-state symptoms and dopaminergic pain modulation may have coexisted.
objects.surviving_point: That mixed-mechanism explanation is compatible with the case architecture. It actually strengthens the need for symptom-specific reconsideration rather than supporting a permanent binary partition.
objects.title: Stage Four — What later evidence bore on the original unresolved relationship?

objects.argument:
The later record is not static. Treatment changes repeatedly. Individual symptoms are reinterpreted. Dopaminergic coverage is altered. A foot phenomenon is later called parkinsonian. Leg pain and shuffling become OFF-related. Morning pain becomes a target of Sinemet CR.

Those are real updates.

But they are predominantly **local updates**: a prescription changes, a symptom is reclassified, a treatment trial is introduced, a dose is altered.

The presently represented record does not show an equally explicit document asking the global historical question again:

- What did the later medication-state evidence do to the original 2017 “Not clear” relationship?
- Did the Podiatry/Neurology partition still describe the case adequately?
- Did the later dystonia and OFF-related findings require the historical foot narrative to be revised?
- Did the PRKN branch alter the explanatory model?
- Which historical foot symptoms remained structural, which became neurologically mediated, and which remained unresolved?

That is the central documentary distinction:

> **The record permitted local updating while the surviving documentary architecture shows less evidence of global updating.**

This proposition is deliberately about the record, not the clinicians' private reasoning.
objects.evidential_status:
**Document-only as a record-architecture proposition.**  
Additional source material could qualify it.

---
objects.question: Did later evidence merely change treatment locally, or did it cause the original 2017 case architecture to be reconstructed?
objects.strongest_alternative_explanation: Global reconsideration may have occurred informally or may have been considered unnecessary because local treatment changes already reflected the clinically relevant updates.
objects.surviving_point: That is possible. The controlled proposition is only that such global reconstruction is not equivalently represented in the surviving documentary record.
objects.title: Stage Five — What happened to the original architecture when contrary or qualifying evidence accumulated?

objects.argument:
The later PRKN result does not retrospectively prove the cause of every historical foot symptom.

Its documentary significance is different.

It confirms that the PARK2/PRKN branch was not an incidental hindsight construction. That branch existed contemporaneously in 2017–2018, was independently strengthened by Prof Healy, remained specifically suspected by Galway, and was eventually genetically confirmed.

Accordingly, later representations of the historical case as simply “idiopathic Parkinson's disease” do not reproduce the full earlier etiological record unless they are understood as syndrome-level shorthand.
objects.question: Does the eventual PRKN result simply add a new diagnosis, or does it also illuminate the earlier documentary branch?
objects.strongest_alternative_explanation: “Idiopathic Parkinson's disease” may have been used loosely or phenomenologically rather than as a formal denial of genetic aetiology.
objects.surviving_point: That may reconcile the language. It does not erase the fact that the earlier documentary record contained a specific genetic hypothesis which later proved etiologically real.
objects.title: Stage Six — What did later genetics do to the historical record?

The record states: “Alcohol is very reduced.”

The record states: “He is smoking but I have asked him to stop please (25 rollies – it is more than it was and the Dopamine agonist may be perpetuating this as most people with iPD find it easier to stop as Prof Healy had observed to him before).”
The record states: “As above, it is extremely difficult to navigate to a "perfect place".”
The record states: “I’m not so worried about deterioration times if he has a cold or flu or he is sick, with something-the Parkinson's will just automatically play up.”

The record states: “What I’m more bothered about is his overall Quality of Life but not disadvantaging him, or putting him at risks from the adverse effects – short medium and long term in trying to balance a difficult situation.”
The record states: “What [Patient] most definitely does need is a very structured regularity in his life style.”
The record states: “That is to say, I don't really want much variation in the times of getting up each day and in the times of application of the patch.”
The record states: “This is because it makes it very difficult to have a longer term interpretation.”
The record states: “Less day-to-day variation in lifecycles is what is needed.”

The record states: “For example if he was on Sinemet and 20-30 years old - if he was varying the first dosage times by 3 hours per day, we would obviously view that in the vast majority of Parkinson's patients as a major problem.”
The record states: “I'm not saying he has to get up at a given time or take that patch at a given time --- but it does need to be fairly standardised to give him/us a larger overview.”
The record states: “This is also underlined by how the procyclidine time is also varying with when he is getting up.”
The record states: “As I have explained to him today, whatever we do with dopamine stimulation is going to interfere with the "tight rope".”

The record states: “This is the balance across on one hand: a lack of movement and being stiff and being uncomfortable versus on the other hand impulsivity; compulsive behaviours; obsessionality - - and indeed as he has already experienced - chorea and worse elements of chorea-dyskinesia.”

The record states: “While the dopamine agonist that he is on at the current time is "artificial" it is far too simple a reduction to say that if he was given the natural product-(Sinemet or Madopar), that he would feel better and feel less "artificial in himself".”

The record states: “(That being said he knows form the very beginning that people do tend to prefer agents like sinement mroeso) It is the standard view across neurology that if we were to let [Patient] have the more "natural product” now, what it would certainly accentuate (especially in one so young) the likelihood that in relatively short order that profoundly troublesome dyskinesia would emerge.”
The record states: “There will come a time or sooner or later Sinemet-levodopa will have to be looked at.”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “Maybe we will be driven to that by obsessionality issues, or whatever---but he is only 41 and therefore it is my preference to try to leave having to look at levodopa for as long as is humanly possible.”
The record states: “I have to be quite clear-[Patient] was not in the least bit pushing for levodopa today.”
The record states: “He never asked for this and he did not bring this question up himself.”
The record states: “He knows all this from before.”
The record states: “He isn’t planning on going back to work right now.”

objects.qualification: This records the administrative or care-pathway act described.
objects.substantive_text: The record states: “Of note he had been fired the day after his original discharge from Hospital.”
The record states: “The circumstances seemed to have been less than ideal.”
The record states: “Ideally we’d like if he could be engaged in work.”
The record states: “All I have asked [Patient] to do today for the moment is to try very much to regularise timings of medications please.”

The record states: “As noted above: It's not just about regularising medication timing it is about trying to regularise lifestyle timing as well I was delighted to see [Patient] back at neurology outpatient’s clinic today.”
The record states: “Everything is as detailed per the summary marked Feb 2019 just above and for brevity I won't reiterate it all.”
The record states: “In simple terms this is going to be a very “tightrope walk” in terms of trying to balance out a whole range of factors.”

The record states: “We haven't really changed anything today (there has been a lot of change in the last 4 months) and this is about trying to achieve a degree of acceptable stability in medications and management.”
The record states: “CLINIC NOVEMEBR 2019 [Patient] was seen by our team and myself at Neurology Consults in AMU on Monday 2017 07 03rd.”
The record states: “I won't reiterate the whole story with a long narrative history because it is very much as per the summary above.”
The record states: “This is really quite long though, and this is in part because some of its purpose is for supply to [Patient].”
The record states: “This is an unusual situation and [Patient] has had a lot of questions most understandably and therefore this is also meant to consolidate a lot of discussions which we have had.”

The record states: “Additionally it is in a way to help (as he termed himself) “with debriefing”; as well as to set out for him a clear plan for the gradual titration onto different treatment modalities.”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “We think that [Patient] unfortunately has a Parkinsonism.”

The record states: “Ordinarily, as you can imagine most individuals are diagnosed with idiopathic Parkinson – very effectively in the community by their General Practitioner and indeed often started on medications.”
The record states: “In the vast majority of cases our role is really to confirm and give the diagnosis and adjust the treatments.”
The record states: “Generally this is achieved in a relatively short outpatient visit and we adjust the person’s medications and just observe how things are.”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “However for very obvious reasons given his very young age at the current time and moreover the possible very young age at onset maybe 13-14 years ago, I have been keen to keep [Patient] in Hospital until we could get an MRI scan.”
The record states: “I'm sorry for the delays in getting this done as an inpatient because obviously he was not prioritised by Radiology as this is a long-standing issue.”
The record states: “However in its own way, this has all suited us and [Patient] very well.”
The record states: “It has allowed us get a lot done with [Patient] and explore a lot of questions in what is obviously a very challenging situation.”
The record states: “He has learned a huge amount for the last week.”

The record states: “Moreover, the treatment options here are somewhat more limited than usual and not as dramatically effective for the person as might usually be the case where Levodopa/Dopamine Agonists may be introduced This longer duration of an admission has helped us have a firmer footing going forward for having a plan of how things will be introduced.”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “Obviously I think it is particularly clear that he has an exceptionally high cognitive baseline and he has taken on things exceedingly well.”

The record states: “Moreover he is well able to say when he is being overwhelmed with too much information but he will carry-over excellently day-to-day and build on what he has learned, and question very appropriately with exceptional insight.”
The record states: “The question of how much information is too much is very valid.”
The record states: “However again this is a circumstance of exceptional insight.”

The record states: “While some of the documentation may be worrying to read, e.g. the risk of dementia in some form of Parkinson’s - - quite simply very quickly anyone could find this information on the internet and I want it to be clear that we are hopeful this will not be the case.”
The record states: “Parkinsons? – Typical / Atypical?”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “We think that the cause is a Parkinson's disease.”
The record states: “However in many respects it is of course an atypical presentation: ###lack of prominent tremor.”
The record states: “Form of Parkinsons/Parkinsonism?”

The record states: “In essence, most Parkinson's disease disorders are disorders of a protein called Synuclein or how Synuclein is handled - - whereas the Parkinson's plus disorders can be disorders of protein Synculein, or range of other protein disorders e.g. very prominently protein Tau.”

The record states: “It is an unpleasant analogy - and of course this is a very sensitive and deeply personal subject--- however an effective practical analogy which I have heard patients come up with themselves is perhaps the nature of: "rust" and rust “spreading”.”
The record states: “Any individual person can conceptulise that rust may be of different forms.”
The record states: “While most people think of iron oxide as “rust” - - we all know that other forms of rust --- depending on the underlying metal --- can develop.”
The record states: “In a similar way, most Parkinson's disease protein abnormalities are of synculein whereas there are other forms of protein abnormalities in some parkinsonian disorders.”

The record states: “Additionally in other conditions there are ways indeed that the same protein can present in different individuals - producing different disease forms (e.g. synuclein disorder also causes MSA and Lewy body disease – quite separately to more ordinary Parkinson’s disease).”
The record states: “Obviously there is a question of whether the previously used recreational drugs may have been a factor.”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “I suppose it is plausible.”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “It is possible that recreational drugs used that may have been quite harmless in the rest of the population but may have accelerated the situation in [Patient] --- however I wouldn't have any great confidence in that explanation.”
The record states: “The larger question is whether the formulation and chemical composition of any of the agents previously used could have caused an MPTP like effect causing his Parkinsonsism.”
The record states: “Again I am reluctant to accept that as an explanation either.”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “I suspect that this was always going to happen to [Patient] and I don’t want him having any idea that this was “caused”.”
The record states: “Himself [Patient] was worried that the alcohol was a factor?”

The record states: “Aside from this being somewhat effective for him as a “de-tensioning” treatment over the years, and notwithstanding that 70 units of alcohol per week can have its own consequences and would not have been helping because of how alcohol can affect DNA repair mechanisms --- I really don't give much credence to the argument that the alcohol was any major factor in this development of a Parkinsonian disorder in [Patient].”
The record reports: “I have explained to him the difficulties with the genetic assessment.”
The record reports: “One of the chief difficulties with this is the question of whether a firm genetic diagnosis will actually actively change management?”
The record states: “This question is (in the majority of cases) usually answered in the negative.”

The record reports: “In a way to explain genetics, I have in a very simplistic manner broken it up into 3 different concepts: -#1 what I term for [Patient]’s understanding as “strong genetics” ---where genetic disorders run very strongly through a family.”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “We would terms these usually Autosomal Dominant.This is clearly not the case in [Patient]'s case and therefore it is not likely that these apply.”
The record states: “It would not apply to most individuals with Parkinson's either.”

The record states: “It is not a worry as he has no children as yet. #2 what I term for for [Patient]’s understanding as "moderate genetics" ---I use this example to explain where a person may have a range of different genes, many of them are currently unknown but which confer “susceptibilities” to Parkinson's.”

The record states: “Depending on the combination of susceptibilities a person has genetically, then these, and various components of environment can contribute to the development of a Parkinson's disorder.”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “This is a theory that probably applies to most people who actually develop Parkinson's disease “sporadically” or “idiopathically” who may have susceptibility genes that we do not understand the role of as yet or known genes with variations (e.g. in the LRRK2/ SNCA / GBA genes), as well as a range of possible environmental factors. #3---what I term for [Patient]’s understanding as "weak genetics"”
The record states: “---by this we mean the classical autosomal recessively inherited disorders that can occur within a family but which would be very unlikely to affect other family members.”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “It is quite plausible that [Patient] may have one of these disorders as the cause for his Parkinsons/Parkinsonisms.”

The record states: “More specifically given a number of issues including his very young age of onset; the akinetic rigidity; the lack of a Dominant family history; and the marked symmetry; as well as how cognitively excellent [Patient] is, there is a question of whether the indicators are that he does have a PRKN gene disorder (PARK 2)?”
The record states: “Nervethless aspects may point to rarer monogenic explanations such as PARK 6 or PARK7 or even PARK 9 (the neuropathy question).”

The record reports: “A summary of where we are with Genetics can be seen from this summary from the National Institutes of health in the US: Genetic Testing in Parkinson's Disease Genetic testing has recently become available for the parkin and PINK1 genes.”
The record states: “Parkin is a large gene and testing is difficult.”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “At the current stage of understanding, testing is likely to give a meaningful result only for people who develop the condition before the age of 30 years.”
The record states: “PINK1 appears to be a rare cause of inherited Parkinson's disease.”
The record states: “A small percentage (~2 percent) of those developing the condition at an early age appear to carry mutations in the PINK1 gene.”
The record reports: “Genetic testing for the PARK7, SNCA and LRRK2 genes is also available.”

The record reports: “Individuals and families who are interested in having genetic testing can learn more about their risk for Parkinson's disease and the availability and accuracy of genetic testing for this disease by setting up an appointment with a genetics health professional.”

The record reports: “Genetic professionals work as members of health care teams providing information and support to individuals or families who have genetic disorders or may be at risk for inherited conditions.”
The record reports: “Genetic professionals can discuss the risks, benefits and limitations of available genetic testing for Parkinson's disease.”

The record reports: “See: Frequently Asked Questions about Genetic Counseling Another article on the genetics of Parkinsons written a couple of years ago from the Department here with [Senior Consultant] is enclosed within.”

The record reports: “Accordingly the only real current value of a "genetic" diagnosis is in terms of what it might tell us about the actual neuropathological form of which neurodegenerative condition he has and maybe to some degree with prognostication and an understanding of Levodopa sensitivities?”

The record reports: “Knowledge of a particular genetic form may help with prognostication - - - but at all times we’ve emphasised to [Patient] the variability in outcomes and limitations in prognostication.”
The record states: “We simply don’t know.”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “In reality, while I am not an expert on these conditions (I am not a movement disorders neurologist) --- however I suspect that whatever testing we might send may well be negative and [Patient] has been prepared for this likelihood.”

The record states: “Additionally there is a question of whether we should just wait and in a number of years do the whole genome or a whole exome analysis when the information underpinning the associations of various genes and various phenotypes has expanded much more from where it is now?”
The record reports: “Whatever form and whatever genetic cause is the cause, the question which is undoubtedly the most important is as regards therapy?”
The record states: “Can we improve how the person is?”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “Ordinarily we would use levodopa or dopamine agonists however in these types of situations we tend to be extremely cautious in their usage for the reasons outlined in the summary on treatment and we will try to leave off on this for as long as possible.”
The record states: “No treatments are proven disease modifying, and all treatments are symptomatic – effective to varying degrees, and we will trying different symptomatic approaches with him first.”
The record states: “Treatment should be view in two ways: 1) Any disease modifying possibilities?”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “There is an unproven theoretical possible benefit giving him CoQ10 and this is started.”
The record states: “Azilect may be disease modifying by slowing whatever trajectory of progression a person is on.”
The record states: “2) Symptomatic therapy to improve his functioning and Quality of Life.”
The record states: “These are per the summary above and I won't reiterate all here for brevity.”
The record states: “However Parkinson's is much more than simply a "movement disorder".”

The record states: “There are multiple other domains which can be affected and which in time may need considerable assistance, and these include urological function, bowel function, sleep function, and mood-affect.”
The record states: “This is an extremely difficult situation.”
The record states: “It is a huge amount to be taken on board – and much more than usual in more ordinary Parkinson’s disease presentations.”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “I think it would be quite obvious that he is particularly very intelligent and he is actually got to grips with things very well.”
The record states: “Moreover, he has a very prescient understanding and will quite appropriately tell us when we are overwhelming with too much information.”
The record states: “Therefore we have tried to introduce things gradually over the last few days/week or so.”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “He has indicated a willingness to be informed in any clinical trials and if we're aware of anything that may be available locally, or more likely with colleagues in Dublin or the UK, and we will refer him to those services should he wish.”
The record reports: “He will have a copy of this letter and it includes information on the rasagiline and also the procyclidine as well as certain genetic aspects of the situation.”

The record states: “I would ask please not to over interpret the list of adverse effects of procyclidine because many of these will have occurred in very much older individuals in himself, or in people a complex psychiatric disorders with parkinsonism is arising from the use of psychiatric agents.”
The record states: “He has been warned of the “nocebo” effect as well.”
The record states: “[Patient] has a good understanding of why we wished to delay the commencement of levodopa or dopamine agonist type treatments at least for now.”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “I think sooner or later we may have to introduce these.”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “It is possible that he will do very well with levodopa and in a sustainable way whenever it is started.”
The record states: “Indeed in time to come - we may regret that we did not start this earlier.”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “However you will understand our delay at the moment as part of the strategy to try to make sure that [Patient] has the best possible long-term outcome.”

The record states: “Certainly, in no way will any individual be disadvantaged from the neuropathological or progression risk perspectives in terms of delaying commencement of the symptomatic treatments.”
The record states: “[Patient] has been given Mr [Parkinson's Nurse]’s contact details for any issues or questions that he has that might arise in the interim.”
The record states: “[This is not an emergency service and [Parkinson's Nurse] is the only Parkinson's nurse in the West of Ireland.”
The record states: “Generally he will try to get back where people leave a message within a couple of days.”
The record states: “[Parkinson's Nurse contact details redacted]] There is a treatment plan as set out above with gradual increase and escalation of procyclidine.”
The record reports: “I'll write to you with any additional investigations that come available especially and most notably the isotope DATscan.”
The record states: “We will hope use these results arriving as a trigger to review the other investigations that have been sent but are not back.”

objects.qualification: This records the administrative or care-pathway act described.
objects.substantive_text: The record states: “[Patient] will have a copy of this letter is well.”
The record states: “In 9/12 at Neurology Clinic.”

objects.qualification: This records the administrative or care-pathway act described.
objects.substantive_text: The record states: “If your patient is not called for followup or does not receive an appointment please contact us.”

The record states: “Nov 2019-11-14th (It has become the understandable preference of some of the General Practitioners to have shorter form letters and therefore all previous details are as per older letters as previously supplied) I was delighted to see [Patient] back at neurology outpatient’s clinic today.”

objects.qualification: This records the administrative or care-pathway act described.
objects.substantive_text: The record states: “In Sept 2019: We had seen [Patient] at the request of the medical assessment unit team on 17 September.”

objects.qualification: This preserves the patient-reported element as recorded by the clinician; it is not restated as an independently verified historical fact.
objects.substantive_text: The clinical record states: “He described a hot patch on the left head and the parietal region 4-5 months and [Patient] had seen [GP] and was diagnosed with C2 problems (very likely correct – i.e.”
The record states: “Gr Occipital neuralgia)).”
The record states: “However the real reason he was there in September was an acute issue with the right shoulder with right shoulder pain.”
The record states: “By 17 September this had been ongoing for 10 days.”
The record states: “He was not sure how it came on.”
The record states: “However it was swiftly worsening.”
The record states: “The pain started mild-but then it got bad.”
The record states: “Nothing would relieve it.”
The record states: “Lying down though was 100% effective and indeed it was still helping him by 10 days after onset.”
The record states: “However when it would start a spasm it could take 4 or 5 minutes to settle down after he would lie down but it would settle.”
The record states: “Sitting as a laptop, sitting to standing, playing darts: he was in big trouble.”
The record states: “There was no obvious injury but he was wondering whether activity at masturbation was a factor.”
The record states: “He does this lying on his back as in flat-not on his side.”
The record states: “9 months beforehand he had started to use a device which reduces physical intensity and usually he would not be using it with his arm - but it was a reasonable consideration.”
The record states: “(There were separate concerns as regards the frequency of masturbation.”
The record states: “This is because of the underlying Parkinson’s diagnosis.”
The record states: “Some days it was not at all-other days it was between 3 and 4 times per day)”

objects.qualification: This preserves the patient-reported element as recorded by the clinician; it is not restated as an independently verified historical fact.
objects.substantive_text: The clinical record states: “Therefore in summary there had been no injury and no fall and he felt that things were worsening.”
The record states: “It had started in the right posterior upper scapula as a focal point and then moved along the shoulder down under the cup of the armpit.”
The record states: “It then would come down the arm down to the anterior bilateral elbow.”
The record states: “At that stage, the examination was really pretty good however he had triceps weakness at grade 4.”
The record states: “In addition wrist extension and finger extension was about grade 5 “minus”.”
The record states: “Reflexes were quite symmetrically intact with essentially normal tone.”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “The impression of myself at that time was whether it was the shoulder or whether it was more likely a radicular problem with spasm perhaps related to a disc?”
The record reports: “I had advised the medical assessment unit team to arrange an MRI of the cervical spine looking especially at the right-sided lower cervical roots.”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “I also advised that an MRI shoulder would be carried out if possible.”
The record reports: “[Patient] was worried then about his ability to be still in an MRI?”
The record states: “Plain paracetamol intravenously had been advised to the medical assessment unit team.”
The record states: “Non-steroidals had failed [Patient].”
The record states: “The shoulder continues to give a lot of trouble.”
The record states: “There has been some changes in it – with some apparent settling but it is far from better.”
The record states: “At the General Practice, [Patient] had been commenced on neurontin gabapentin.”
The record states: “That sort of changed the phenomenology somewhat.”
The record states: “I will describe this in a little bit more detail below.”
The record reports: “The MRI had not been done in the medical assessment unit after we had seen him that day.”
The record states: “It had already been booked and transferred to outpatient booking (but this is at an indeterminate time as an OP booking) and then he was discharged on plain paracetamol.”
The record reports: “The MRI has not happened in the interim.”
The record reports: “Back then, [Patient] had been deeply concerned that he would not be able to stay still for the MRI.”
The record states: “This was understandable given the amount of pain and the acute severity of the pain at the time.”
The record states: “However, even at the moment, he still has very significant concerns as regards whether he would be able to stay still.”
The record states: “This is not simply about the pain in the shoulder.”

The record states: “It is about the general urge to move-the restlessness and the “dystonia” type elements While he explains he would do his level best to keep still, [Patient] cannot be confident that he would be able to do so.”
The record states: “In fairness, as he was there sitting with me today, although he could not remotely be described as either dystonic or dyskinetic, there was a lot of movement.”
The record states: “It wasn’t severe but it was within the descriptors of an akathesic restlessness – though mildly so.”
The record states: “Therefore it is easy to see and understand why there could be a lot of difficulty with him being able to sit still.”
The record reports: “He is prepared to accept the risks of a general anaesthetic to have the MRI done.”

The record reports: “In reality, I have to say that I have never seen anybody have an aspiration in this context, or indeed have an adverse outcome with an MRI under general anaesthesia ---- but we have to mention risks.”
The record reports: “I have rebooked the MRI to be done under general anaesthetic please.”
The record states: “That actually might happen sooner than the ordinary waiting list which he seems to be on.”
The record reports: “[Patient] asked a very salient question as regards whether MRI is the only way to understand what is going on up in the neck and shoulder?”
The record states: “In reality it is not.”

The record reports: “Theoretically, neurophysiology might be helpful but as I have explained to him with an image of the brachial plexus, in reality other modalities do not approach the ability of MRI to be able to find a cause, given the complexity of that region.”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “Certainly it is possible that the MRI will not show anything wrong with his shoulder and will not show anything wrong with the nerve roots or the brachial plexus.”
The record states: “But it is the best structural way we have.”

The record reports: “Neurophysiology, CT, PET, Isotope scans all have particular roles and utilities but they don’t approach the imaging ability of MRI to find the cause - - if there is a cause to be found , or if it is diagnosable based on MRI.”
The record states: “In point of fact, [Patient] had already explained that he does not really care about the cause-e.g. if it is a trapped nerve of the shoulder issue.”

The record states: “However he has very very particular focused concerns as regards whether this may be a malignancy based on the experience of an acquaintance who had similar symptoms who ultimately was demonstrated to have a disseminated malignancy.”

objects.qualification: This preserves the patient-reported element as recorded by the clinician; it is not restated as an independently verified historical fact.
objects.substantive_text: The clinical record states: “As he says, “I can deal with anything”---but [Patient] would like to know.”
The record states: “As I have explained to him it is highly unlikely that it is a malignancy however of course theoretically it is not impossible.”
The record states: “Usually if this was to be a malignancy it would have to be an apical tumour of the right lung.”
The record states: “There is heavy smoking which is a cancer risk no matter how clear his lungs sound in the General Practice.”
The record states: “A Plain CXR was negative back then.”
The record states: “However you will be well aware that of course plain x-rays are a very limited tool for excluding lung cancer.”

The record states: “Nevertheless as was explained to [Patient], if the situation was such that there was a malignancy severe enough to be able to cause this, there is a very high probability that a chest x-ray would find it.”
The record states: “If there was such a malignancy that was infiltrating up into his brachial plexus in such a way as to cause this sort of issue, he should have weakness (much more than he has).”
The record states: “In broad terms, his power is absolutely excellent.”
The record states: “However where it falls down is at the triceps.”
The record states: “He makes a good effort.”
The record states: “But at best it would be called grade 4.”
The record states: “Also it did not hurt while I was doing it and therefore this was not some degree of give way weakness.”
The record states: “The pattern of weakness is not really a “Parkinson’s” type phenomenon.”
The record states: “The way things have changed is also a sensitivity around the LEFT pectoral region.”

objects.qualification: This preserves the patient-reported element as recorded by the clinician; it is not restated as an independently verified historical fact.
objects.substantive_text: The clinical record states: “When the pain hits there is a need to exhale He thinks there is some wasting around the triceps.”
The record states: “There might be a bit.”
The record states: “However predominant interest was actually whether he had any fasciculations.”
The record states: “None are evident.”
The record states: “The power examination is as detailed.”
The record states: “This demonstrates the triceps extension power issue.”
The record states: “This is the same as it was in September and it is quite real, and reproducible and he knows, especially form darts exactly that it is a triceps problem.”
The record states: “The wrist extension is actually really close to perfect.”

The record states: “The bundle begins with Dr Monaghan's 25 March 2025 response to the hospital complaint and then identifies: - Appendix 1: his current working clinical document file containing older information up to approximately 10 March 2025; - Appendix 2: Mr Moloney's complaint/account; - later complaint-response and governance material supplied in support of the clinician's July 2025 regulatory response.”

The record states: “Dr Monaghan states in the bundle that his working file was being supplied so that the documentary basis of his clinical reasoning could be reviewed and that the material included records going back to 2017.”

The record reports: “The working clinical file reproduces the 2017 presentation and examination, including: - longstanding lower-limb tension and later corns/calluses and foot pain; - markedly increased tone, gross bradykinesia and a strikingly abnormal gait; - a footdrop-like appearance described as somewhat suggestive of a dystonic posture and expressly not foot drop; - pes planus and hammertoes; - severe young-onset parkinsonism with an open atypical/genetic differential; - later abnormal DaTSCAN evidence of bilateral dopaminergic deficit.”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “The same reproduced 2017 record states that the leg symptoms, corns/calluses and burning “may have been completely separate” or possibly related to a peripheral neuropathy and records the conclusion “Not clear.””
The record states: “The plan then separately requests outpatient Chiropody/Podiatry services and records that an SHO had tried to arrange this in hospital.”
The record states: “This bundle is a 2025 reproduction of the clinician's working record.”
The record states: “It is primary evidence of what Dr Monaghan supplied in 2025 and strong documentary evidence of the content of his retained working file.”
The record states: “Where the repository already holds contemporaneous 2017 source pages, those earlier records remain the preferable source for proving the 2017 event itself.”

The record states: “The reproduced 2017 material records a plan to proceed cautiously with conventional dopaminergic therapy because of Liam's very young age and concern about dyskinesia and impulse-control complications.”

The record states: “It also records that the case had been considered at a Neurology Complex Case meeting and that care with later levodopa/dopamine-agonist treatment had been advised with Prof Counihan and Neurology colleagues.”

objects.qualification: This records a clinical opinion or assessment; it is not restated here as an objective conclusion.
objects.substantive_text: The clinician recorded: “The same 2017 working record expressly raises a possible PRKN / PARK2 explanation because of the very young onset, symmetry, akinetic-rigid presentation, lack of a dominant family history and preserved cognition.”
The record states: “It records that PRKN/PARK2 testing or a broader panel was a reasonable option and refers to Prof Healy's interest in that possibility.”
The record states: “The 2017 material establishes that PRKN/PARK2 was a contemporaneous diagnostic possibility, not that a PRKN diagnosis had been made.”
The record reports: “The later 2026 specialist genetic result is a separate evidential origin establishing the eventual genetic diagnosis.”
The record states: “The working file reproduces the 24 April 2018 Neurology record.”

The record states: “It states that the Parkinson nurse had suggested stopping Procyclidine for approximately two weeks in Sept/Oct 2017 because of blurred vision and that, during that stop: “the first thing he noticed changing and changing rapidly was the return on the foot, of the outside left corn.””
The record states: “The same passage records that symptoms worsened somewhat and that Liam was more “shifty” and “unrelaxed” off Procyclidine.”
The record states: “This is the same early treatment-response episode separately represented in the repository's 2018 Neurology source page and contemporaneous 24 October 2017 patient email.”

The record states: “The working file reproduces the 2020 Neurology material describing: - a bad corn on the outside of the left foot; - a left lower-limb “throw” with preserved dorsiflexion, plantarflexion, inversion and eversion power; - the clinician's conclusion that this foot-throw appearance was parkinsonian rather than true foot drop; - exquisite sensitivity of the feet; - excessive movement and urge to move the feet.”
The record states: “These are later direct clinical observations and should not be treated as retrospective proof that every component of the 2017 foot syndrome was neurological.”

The record states: “The working file reproduces the October 2021 clinical record stating that ordinary Sinemet had first been introduced in September 2021 and increased as Kemadrin was withdrawn because of ocular-pressure/visual concerns.”
The record states: “The same record says Liam had been fully counselled and would receive a copy at home, followed by the categorical statement: “the DBS is only ever for the tremor element.”
The record states: “It will not help with anything else.””
The record states: “A narrower patient-specific clinical judgment may have been intended, but this bundle preserves the categorical wording actually recorded and supplied to the patient.”

The record states: “The opening complaint response states that Sinemet had been known to reduce Liam's experience of pain and that Dr Monaghan's own 10 March 2025 Sinemet CR prescription was “also to try to help the morning experience including of pain.””
The record states: “It further records that the recent Sinemet CR escalation had provided “profound relief currently.””

The record states: “The clinician's explanation remains that pain could have mixed or peripheral causes and that Parkinsonism/dopaminergic state could magnify the experience of pain; the response also preserves the stated rationale for cautious dose escalation in a young patient because of dyskinesia and dopamine-dysregulation/impulse-control risks.”

The record states: “Across the working file Dr Monaghan repeatedly states that his long clinic letters were intended to be copied to Liam and to create a shared understanding of what had been discussed, why decisions had been made and when.”
The record states: “This is evidence about the information framework the treating clinician says he deliberately supplied.”
The record states: “It does not prove that Liam agreed with every proposition or that every discussion was fully understood in the same way by clinician and patient.”

The record states: “This bundle is especially useful for source genealogy because it shows which historical clinical records and propositions Dr Monaghan himself selected and supplied in 2025 when explaining and defending the earlier management.”
The record states: “It must not be counted as independent corroboration of historical propositions merely because those propositions reappear inside a later regulatory bundle.”

# 12 June 2025 — GDPR Article 16 Rectification Request
**Source type:** primary contemporaneous patient / data-subject email
**Author:** Liam Moloney
**Recipients:** HSE DPO; DDPO West copied
**Date:** 12 June 2025
**Subject:** `GDPR Rectification Request – Patient Liam Moloney (DOB: 12/11/1977)`
**Provenance:** read directly from the connected Gmail account. This page is a redacted transcription of the message body. No analytical findings are made on this page.
Dear Data Protection Officer,

I am writing under Article 16 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) to formally request rectification and annotation of inaccurate personal data held about me within Galway University Hospitals.

Between 2017 and 2025, I was under the care of your Neurology Department, where I was assigned a diagnosis of idiopathic Parkinson’s disease. However, this diagnosis was reached without incorporating or exploring my primary presenting symptom: bilateral foot pain, which began in 2004–2005 and was the basis for my GP referral in 2017.

In 2025, following my own adjustment of dopaminergic medication (Sinemet CR), I experienced immediate and sustained relief of that symptom — effectively disproving the previously presumed peripheral neuropathy and revealing that the symptom was dopamine-responsive all along.
This finding invalidates critical assumptions underpinning the diagnosis recorded and disseminated across my medical history.
Under Article 16 of GDPR, I am entitled to request rectification where my data is:
- Inaccurate (e.g., omission of key symptom in referral/consultation notes),
- Misleading (e.g., implication of peripheral neuropathy without confirmatory testing),
- Or incomplete in a clinically significant way (e.g., diagnosis recorded as conclusive despite absence of diagnostic levodopa trial).

The long-standing diagnostic label in my file — and its downstream replication — does not reflect the full, accurate clinical picture, especially now that a dopamine-responsive mechanism has been demonstrated.
1. Rectify all relevant documents where the absence of my core symptom (severe, disabling foot pain) misrepresents my diagnostic journey.

2. Annotate all files (referrals, discharge summaries, diagnostic letters) that present a conclusive Parkinson’s diagnosis, noting the lack of dopaminergic diagnostic trial and the subsequent contradictory evidence in 2025.
3. Preserve all internal and external records relating to my case for further review, including MDT notes, email correspondence, and meeting records.
This request is made in good faith, in pursuit of factual accuracy and the correction of records that continue to influence how my health condition is understood, managed, and recorded.
Please confirm receipt of this request and respond within the statutory time frame of one calendar month.
Sincerely,
Liam Moloney

**Redaction note:** Home address, date of birth, patient ID and telephone number have been omitted from this repository transcription. The original Gmail message remains the controlling source. Statements about diagnosis, causation and disproving prior assumptions are the data subject's assertions in the request, not findings made by this source page.

# 6 September 2025 — Article 16 decision concerning clinical records
**Source type:** primary institutional/data-governance decision
**Author/signatory:** Nuala Madden, SARS Co-ordinator, University Hospital Galway
**Recipient:** Liam Moloney
**Date:** 6 September 2025
**Provenance:** transcribed from the primary PDF `Sept 6th Refusal.pdf` preserved in Gmail and directly read in the project.
**Status:** faithful redacted transcription of the substantive decision. The original PDF remains the controlling source. No analytical findings are made on this page.
Dear Mr Moloney,

I refer to your request made on 12th June, 2025 for the erasure of a record, held in your medical file at Galway University Hospital. Firstly, I wish to apologise for the delay in issuing you a decision.
Your request in summary refers to the following:
1. “Rectify all relevant documents where the absence of my core symptoms (severe, disabling foot pain) misrepresents my diagnostic journey.”

2. “Annotate all files (referrals, discharge summaries, diagnostic letters) that present a conclusive Parkinson’s diagnosis, noting the lack of dopaminergic diagnostic trial and subsequent evidence in 2025.”
The decision has been made that the personal information contained in your medical records to which your application refers is not judged to be misleading for the following reasons.

The HSE relies on Articles 6 and 9 of the GDPR as the legal basis for processing a patient’s personal and medical data. Article 6(1)(e) of GDPR is relied upon for processing the individual’s personal data which states that processing shall be lawful if “processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller”. For the HSE this lawful authority is vested in us through the Health Act 2004.

Sections 36(1) & 52(1) of the Act cover suitable and specific measures of processing and of special categories of personal data for the provision of healthcare. I am satisfied that the HSE has met its legal requirements under the Act and is in compliance with GDPR.

A diagnosis in a medical file is the reflection of the professional opinion of the doctor at that moment of time and based on the information available to that moment in time. On this basis the HSE has a lawful basis for continued processing of your medical records in accordance with Article 7(1) of GDPR.

As a consequence, it remains factually accurate to record the opinion or diagnosis that was made and what the opinion or diagnosis was, such data would not be “inaccurate” as it is a factually accurate reflection that an opinion or diagnosis occurred and what the opinion or diagnosis was at that point in time and is still necessary in relation to the purposes for which the personal data was originally collected or otherwise processed and is consistent with Article 17(3)(c) in providing comprehensive medical assessment and treatment of the individual.

In addition, a medical opinion or diagnosis provides important context for any subsequent medical treatment decisions made by Health Care providers. A prior opinion or diagnosis may explain why certain medications were prescribed or certain treatment plans were undertaken. Maintaining the medical record in its current form, serves the public interest by ensuring the service user and the treating Healthcare Professionals have a reliable record of what has taken place.

Following consideration of the provisions of the above legislation, it has been decided to refuse your request, as there is an obligation on the HSE and its staff to keep accurate records which are essential for the continuity of care and comprehensive enough to allow Health Practitioners to be fully informed of factors which impact on the provision of care to be provided.
Rights to appeal
If you are unhappy with this decision you may make a complaint in writing to the Office of the Data Protection Commission.
Yours sincerely,
Nuala Madden
SARS Co-ordinator,
University Hospital Galway.

**Redaction / scope note:** postal addresses, signature image and administrative footer are omitted. This is the clinical-record Article 16 decision. It is distinct from the separate 6 September 2025 QPS closure-letter decision.
# 6 September 2025 - Article 16 decision concerning QPS closure letters
**Source type:** primary administrative / data-rights decision
**Author/signatory:** Nuala Madden, SARS Coordinator, Galway University Hospitals
**Recipient:** Liam Moloney
**Date:** 6 September 2025
**Underlying request:** Article 16 request dated 15 June 2025 concerning QPS closure letters
**Provenance:** transcribed from the original two-page PDF preserved as `Sept 6th refusal II.pdf`, located in the connected Gmail account and directly read.
**Status:** faithful redacted transcription. The original PDF remains the controlling source. No analytical findings are made on this page.
Dear Mr. Moloney,
I refer to your request dated 15th June, 2025 made under Article 16 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) for the:
> “Immediate rectification of all Quality and Patient Safety (QPS) ‘closure letters’ issued by Galway University Hospital that
> - Invoke the Health Act 2004 as justification for rerouting complaints back to the original clinician; and
> - Use the term ‘assessment’ to describe an undocumented non-transparent internal process that classifies complaints as ‘solely clinical’ without independent review or appeal.”

I wish to advise that the GDPR does provide individuals with the right to rectification of inaccurate personal data and the right to erasure in specific circumstances. However, your request does not seem to relate to the rectification of your personal data.

Personal data as defined under the GDPR means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person (‘data subject’); therefore a Quality and Patient Safety “closure letters” issued by Galway University Hospital does not relate to you as a data subject.

Therefore, my decision is to refuse this request for the amendment of records, as it does not relate to your personal data and does not come within the scope of personal data as defined under the GDPR.
If you are unhappy with this decision, you may make a complaint in writing to the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner.
Yours sincerely,
Nuala Madden
SARS Coordinator
Galway University Hospitals

objects.substantive_text: 2. **Failure to Reassess**

objects.source_family: Formal Complaint – Diagnostic Anchoring, Bias, and Failure to Reassess (2017–2025)
objects.substantive_text: - Despite deterioration, ongoing pain, and functional impairment, no fresh neurological workup was undertaken that considered Parkinson’s-related pain syndromes or tested dopaminergic responsiveness.

objects.source_family: Formal Complaint – Diagnostic Anchoring, Bias, and Failure to Reassess (2017–2025)
objects.substantive_text: 3. **Potential Hierarchical Influence**

objects.source_family: Formal Complaint – Diagnostic Anchoring, Bias, and Failure to Reassess (2017–2025)
objects.substantive_text: - I have reason to believe senior clinical influence may have advised caution against certain treatments, which—combined with referral bias—closed off viable therapeutic trials.

objects.source_family: Formal Complaint – Diagnostic Anchoring, Bias, and Failure to Reassess (2017–2025)
objects.substantive_text: ### The Turning Point

objects.source_family: Formal Complaint – Diagnostic Anchoring, Bias, and Failure to Reassess (2017–2025)
objects.substantive_text: In March 2025, I independently trialed Sinemet CR. The result was immediate and sustained relief from two decades of disabling foot pain—effectively disproving the prior working diagnosis and suggesting my condition was dopamine-responsive all along.

objects.source_family: Formal Complaint – Diagnostic Anchoring, Bias, and Failure to Reassess (2017–2025)
objects.substantive_text: This raises a fundamental question: Why was this possibility not explored earlier, given the magnitude of harm endured?

objects.source_family: Formal Complaint – Diagnostic Anchoring, Bias, and Failure to Reassess (2017–2025)
objects.substantive_text: ### The Harm Caused

objects.source_family: Formal Complaint – Diagnostic Anchoring, Bias, and Failure to Reassess (2017–2025)
objects.substantive_text: - Physical: Prolonged, preventable pain

objects.source_family: Formal Complaint – Diagnostic Anchoring, Bias, and Failure to Reassess (2017–2025)
objects.substantive_text: - Psychological: Fear of movement, cumulative distress, and erosion of resilience

objects.source_family: Formal Complaint – Diagnostic Anchoring, Bias, and Failure to Reassess (2017–2025)
objects.substantive_text: - Loss of Trust: A profound impact on my confidence in clinical systems' ability to self-correct

objects.source_family: Formal Complaint – Diagnostic Anchoring, Bias, and Failure to Reassess (2017–2025)
objects.substantive_text: ### Request for Review and Disclosure

objects.source_family: Formal Complaint – Diagnostic Anchoring, Bias, and Failure to Reassess (2017–2025)
objects.substantive_text: I make no presumptions about individual intent or malice. My concern is systemic: that processes of diagnostic framing, confirmation bias, and deference to hierarchy may have overridden patient experience and clinical curiosity.

objects.source_family: Formal Complaint – Diagnostic Anchoring, Bias, and Failure to Reassess (2017–2025)
objects.substantive_text: I respectfully request:

objects.source_family: Formal Complaint – Diagnostic Anchoring, Bias, and Failure to Reassess (2017–2025)
objects.substantive_text: 1. An independent review of my case, with attention to the clinical reasoning applied from 2017 to 2025.

objects.source_family: Formal Complaint – Diagnostic Anchoring, Bias, and Failure to Reassess (2017–2025)
objects.substantive_text: 2. Full disclosure of my medical records, referrals, specialist correspondence, and any internal memos related to my case during this period.

objects.source_family: Formal Complaint – Diagnostic Anchoring, Bias, and Failure to Reassess (2017–2025)
objects.substantive_text: 3. A written response explaining how this outcome was possible, and what measures exist to prevent similar diagnostic anchoring from persisting unchecked in other cases.

objects.source_family: Formal Complaint – Diagnostic Anchoring, Bias, and Failure to Reassess (2017–2025)
objects.substantive_text: 4. Preservation of all records related to my case, including internal communications, pending my full review.

objects.source_family: Formal Complaint – Diagnostic Anchoring, Bias, and Failure to Reassess (2017–2025)
objects.substantive_text: ### Closing Statement

objects.source_family: Formal Complaint – Diagnostic Anchoring, Bias, and Failure to Reassess (2017–2025)
objects.substantive_text: I submit this complaint not in anger, but from a place of humility and genuine need for understanding.

objects.source_family: Formal Complaint – Diagnostic Anchoring, Bias, and Failure to Reassess (2017–2025)
objects.substantive_text: I recognise the pressures and complexities of medical practice. However, after eight years of persistent pain and the eventual discovery that relief was possible, I am compelled to ask how the system could have missed this—despite my continued engagement.

objects.source_family: Formal Complaint – Diagnostic Anchoring, Bias, and Failure to Reassess (2017–2025)
objects.substantive_text: My aim is not confrontation, but to ensure learning, accountability, and the protection of future patients from similar harm.

objects.source_family: Formal Complaint – Diagnostic Anchoring, Bias, and Failure to Reassess (2017–2025)
objects.substantive_text: Yours sincerely,

objects.source_family: Formal Complaint – Diagnostic Anchoring, Bias, and Failure to Reassess (2017–2025)
objects.substantive_text: Liam Moloney

Dear Mr Moloney,

Thank you for your communication via email. I am sorry to learn of your difficulties. As I have not been involved in your care, I have forwarded your communication to your consultant Dr Thomas Monaghan, copied herein also. Given the concerns raised in your communication, I believe he will forward these to the Patient Advocacy Department within the hospital who will investigate the matter with due process.
Yours sincerely,
Dr. Timothy Counihan
Consultant Neurologist
**CC recorded on original:** Liam's GP and Dr Thomas Monaghan.

# 13 January 2026 — DPC re-engagement suggestion
**Source type:** primary regulatory correspondence
**Author:** Niamh Bourke, Complaint Assessment & Early Resolution Unit, Data Protection Commission
**Recipient:** Liam Moloney
**Date:** 13 January 2026
**Reference:** C-25-7-2074
**Provenance:** transcribed from the primary DPC correspondence preserved in the connected Gmail archive.
**Status:** faithful redacted transcription of the substantive correspondence. The original email remains controlling. No analytical findings are made on this page.

The DPC confirmed that the complaint had been transferred to its Complaint Assessment and Early Resolution Unit and explained that assessment may require copies of rights requests, reminders, supporting documents and relevant correspondence.

The DPC suggested reviewing the material already submitted and providing anything omitted. It also suggested that, if not already done, Liam might contact University Hospital Galway to tell it that a DPC complaint had been submitted, as this might prompt resolution and potentially speed matters.

**Source-boundary note:** This correspondence establishes the DPC’s procedural suggestion and complaint status. It is not a merits finding on the Article 16/18 issues and does not determine whether any GDPR breach occurred.
# 16 February 2026 — DPC notification concerning renewed Article 16 / 18 engagement
**Source type:** primary data-subject correspondence to regulator
**Date:** 16 February 2026
**Subject:** `C-25-7-2074 — Article 12(3) Expiry Notification (Renewed Article 16 / 18 Engagement)`
**Provenance:** complete substantive text supplied to the project.
**Status:** redacted source transcription. Original Gmail message remains controlling. No analytical findings are made on this page.
The data subject notified the Data Protection Commission that the renewed Article 16 / Article 18 engagement of 14 January 2026 had, in his view, passed the one-month Article 12(3) response period.
The message stated that as of 16 February 2026:
- no acknowledgment had been received from the controller;
- no extension notice had been issued; and
- no substantive response had been provided.
It asked the Commission to determine whether the controller was compliant with Article 12(3) and with its handling obligations under Articles 16 and 18.

**Source-boundary note:** This source proves that the non-response position was reported to the DPC on 16 February 2026. Whether a legal deadline had expired, whether Article 18 remained in force, and whether any breach occurred are legal questions not determined by this correspondence alone.

Liam

Dear Mr Moloney,

I am writing to you in respect of the complaint you made in relation to Dr Timothy Counihan received on 9 May 2025. Under the Medical Practitioners Act 2007, as amended (“the Act”), complaints are made to, and investigated by, the Chief Executive Officer (“CEO”) of the Medical Council.
Please note that the CEO has made a decision not to investigate your complaint against Dr Counihan. The CEO’s decision and the basis for it are explained further below.
Before a decision is made to investigate a complaint, the CEO is required to consider whether he or she:
i. is satisfied that the complaint is not made in good faith, or
ii. is satisfied that the complaint is frivolous or vexatious.

If the CEO decides that a complaint comes within one of the above categories, the complaint will be closed. If the complaint does not come within one of these categories, then the CEO is required to investigate the complaint.

The CEO has considered this complaint and decided that the complaint was frivolous and/or vexatious in circumstances where Dr Counihan was **not directly involved in your care** and was satisfied that the complaint did not raise any clinical concerns or patient safety issues in relation to Dr Counihan and could never reach the threshold of seriousness to warrant a referral to the Fitness to Practise Committee.
Please note that the CEO has made a decision not to investigate your complaint against Dr Counihan. On that basis, no further action will be taken in relation to your complaint against Dr Counihan.
An Authorised Officer will be in touch with you in due course in relation to your complaint against Dr Thomas Monaghan.
Please note that a copy of your complaint together with the CEO’s decision outlined above has also been sent to Dr Counihan for his information.

# 29 July 2025 - Dr Thomas Monaghan submission to the Medical Council
**Source type:** primary later clinician/regulatory submission
**Author:** Dr Thomas Monaghan, Consultant Neurologist
**Recipient:** Ms Gemma Fallon, Authorised Officer of the CEO, Medical Council of Ireland
**Reference:** R / 016 / 25
