Dear Ms Fallon,
Thank you for your letter.
I am of course personally devastated to be in receipt of this.

However that is not what matters: It is the experience of the person that is at the heart of this that matters, and it is the assessment and the judgement of the Medical Council in your role to protect patients, that matters.

Mr Moloney made a complaint to University Hospital Galway in March 2025. I answered this immediately to the best of my ability to the Hospital, and in the knowledge that that reply would be copied to Mr Moloney. Mr Moloney had specified he did not want to have contact with clinicians until he was in receipt of what he requested.

The Hospital supplied me with a subsequent complaint on the 24th of April 2025. Due to technical issues, I was delayed in sending the reply to the Hospital in respect of this until the evening of the 25th of April 2025.

On the 28th of April 2025, while the second complaint was in process with University Hospital Galway, I was informed by the Hospital of a third complaint - a re-framing as he explained of the first complaint.
In answering each of the first two complaints: I have at length explained my thinking and my medical management of Mr Moloney's medical needs as per attached.
I believe these to have been correct and appropriate.
I understand and respect that Mr Moloney does not agree.

If I may summarise what I believe to be my understanding of his position in the complaints received in the Hospital: this is that I have framed everything in the context of an unproven neuropathy, being the cause of his symptoms, and I have “blamed alcohol”.
I think there is prima facie evidence as per the documentation enclosed, that this is not correct.
I think the detailed explanations explored in my responses to his complaints make this clear.

In point of fact Mr Moloney has been on treatment with Levodopa (Sinemet) since 2021 and in another forms, and we have known and documented that his has had a beneficial response for him in terms of pain. We had also tried to used synthetic Dopamine agents since 2018 (discontinued due to adverse effect/intolerances related to dopaminergic treatment)
His contention would seem to be that “Sinemet CR” (Controlled release Levodopa) started earlier would have given him sooner relief of pain and other leg based symptoms).
To be of assistance to the Medical Council I have enclosed all of the documentation to answer Mr Moloney's complaints, that I have supplied to the University Hospital Galway.
In Particular there is:
- SECTION 1 - The reply to Mr Moloney's first complaint. This explains in detail my clinical reasoning.
- This also includes (APPENDIX 1) the working document of his clinical records that I have going back to 2017.

- I asked the Hospital to provide my response to his complaint letter, unedited and un-redacted to Mr Moloney (as opposed to a draft of a Hospital Response letter formulated incorporating parts of my answers). I asked the Hospital to provide all of my working file - he requested his data, and he is of course completely entitled to this. (APPENDIX 1). This was to save Mr Moloney having to go through a separate FoI process, so he could have much of the data that he requested, and at speed.
- In APPENDIX 2 - I have enclosed Mr Moloney's original complaint to the Hospital.

- In APPENDIX 3 - I have the reply that was formulated to his additional complaint and his additional questions, when Mr Moloney expressed he was dissatisfied with the Hospital's response and closure of his case (sent by me to the Hospital on the 25th of April 2025).

- In APPENDIX 4 - I have the reply formulated to Mr Moloney's re-framing third complaint to the Hospital. It was at this time I became aware of Mr Moloney's letter to a Neurology colleague Prof Timothy J Counihan, of his concerns as regards Prof Counihan’s advice to myself (in 2017 when we had reviewed Mr Moloney's care at our Neurology Dept Weekly Complex Case meeting). Prof Counihan had no further involvement formally or otherwise in the management of Mr Moloney’s care. Prof Counihan’s advice to myself of that time was only what I already knew to be the case: the necessity for care in the commencement/escalation of Levodopa treatment in a younger person with Parkinsons Disease.

- It was at this time (28th April 2025) that I became aware of the complaint that had been made to the Medical Council, and accordingly a draft of this current document was commenced as of the 28th of April 2025, in anticipation of your now current request of 29th July 2025.
- APPENDIX 5 - Email to the Directorate of Medicine UHG
- APPENDIX 6 - GDPR request for Mr Moloney to have his Medical Records Changed or Annotated.
- (Appendix 7 - the Medical Council complaint - not enclosed, this document is reply)
I accept I may be wrong - but I think and hope that my management was correct.

From 2017, from Mr Moloney's very first inpatient evaluation - I had noted and explored with him that we would try to delay treatment with Levodopa for as long as possible, and then we would also try to delay escalation.
Indeed it was also discussed back then that he may not be happy with this delay.
This was in an effort to protect his overall health and wellbeing in the most holistic of manners. This was only done sincerely, and with his best interests at heart.

Specifically this was to avoid the risk of Dopamine treatment related complications, such as Dyskinesias (abnormal movements); Dopaminergic treatment related Impulse Control disorders / Dopa Dysregulation Syndrome.

Quite simply there is no other conceivable reason that a doctor could or would wish to delay treatment with an agent for symptomatic relief, other than to try to protect the person from adverse outcome.
This was my goal: to try to protect him from the effects of a treatment that we all knew and understood that Mr Moloney would come to need more and more of over time.
As the extensive documentation provided will show evidence of, at every step of the process in his annual reviews, everything that I explored and explained was as documented.
In each instance Mr Moloney was kept aware of everything by this being explained, and his being copied on his own letters.
In the rest of this particular document, to you as the Medical Council, I have not sought to answer the specifics of Mr Moloney’s complaints as we understood them already.

This is simply because I have explored this complex matter which has extended over the 8 years since I have known Mr Moloney, in the detailed answers to his complaints as attached in the associated document.
I have left this in because there has been an evolution of the complaints that Mr Moloney has made.
I am ethically bound and I understand legally bound in terms of "open disclosure" to lay out all the facts/interpretations as I know them to be.

Because Mr Moloney’s complaints to the Medical Council may further evolve, beyond the documentation you provided me with dated the 25th of April, I have therefore enclosed all of this documentation (clinical and complaint management), in the interests of full disclosure.
However to more specifically address aspects of the items from the complaint dated 25th of April 2025, that the Medical Council has supplied me with today 2025-07-29th

**CC: Prof Dan Healy, Consultant Neurologist, Beaumont Hospital, Dublin 9**
Dear Dan,
I wonder if I might seek your advice please as regards Mr Moloney.
Liam is remarkable young man who progressed very far on Channel 4s Countdown in recent years.
Unfortunately Liam seems to have had symptoms of Parkinson's for the last 13 years. He is now age 39 at current presentation, and this is his first time being seen by Neurology.
I would be grateful for advice on what genetic testing might be appropriate in the circumstances and more particularly, whether you thing this is reasonable and likely to help Liam?
In particular would you have genetic contacts who might analyse DNA? UHG will pay wherever the NCMG send samples of course. I have looked at Centogenes proposals as enclosed.
I have his imaging enclosed on disc.
If you felt it might be of benefit to him to be seen in Dublin, Liam would be happy to be seen publically or privately for a once off opinion.
**Myself and Tim are keen to hold back on Levodopa insofar as maybe possible unless you'd advise otherwise?**
We have made a Video which Liam had consented to for Clinical Purposes only - - - and this includes the condition of provision to Beaumont for a second opinion.
With thanks and kind regards,
Thomas

# 29 July 2025 — Dr Thomas Monaghan supporting documentation bundle
**Source type:** primary later clinician/regulatory source bundle containing reproduced earlier clinical records and complaint material
**Supplying clinician:** Dr Thomas Monaghan, Consultant Neurologist
**Date supplied:** 29 July 2025
**File inspected:** `Redacted Supporting documentation rec'd from Dr Thomas Monghan dated 29.07.25.pdf`
**Length:** 185 pages
**Provenance:** the complete PDF was supplied directly to the project and inspected in rendered form and parsed text.

**Status:** source-bundle index only. The original PDF remains the controlling source. This page does not convert reproduced historical material into a new independent evidential origin and makes no medico-legal finding.
The bundle begins with Dr Monaghan's 25 March 2025 response to the hospital complaint and then identifies:
- **Appendix 1:** his current working clinical document file containing older information up to approximately 10 March 2025;
- **Appendix 2:** Mr Moloney's complaint/account;
- later complaint-response and governance material supplied in support of the clinician's July 2025 regulatory response.

Dr Monaghan states in the bundle that his working file was being supplied so that the documentary basis of his clinical reasoning could be reviewed and that the material included records going back to 2017.
The working clinical file reproduces the 2017 presentation and examination, including:
- longstanding lower-limb tension and later corns/calluses and foot pain;
- markedly increased tone, gross bradykinesia and a strikingly abnormal gait;
- a footdrop-like appearance described as somewhat suggestive of a dystonic posture and expressly **not foot drop**;
- pes planus and hammertoes;
- severe young-onset parkinsonism with an open atypical/genetic differential;
- later abnormal DaTSCAN evidence of bilateral dopaminergic deficit.

The same reproduced 2017 record states that the leg symptoms, corns/calluses and burning **“may have been completely separate”** or possibly related to a peripheral neuropathy and records the conclusion **“Not clear.”**
The plan then separately requests outpatient Chiropody/Podiatry services and records that an SHO had tried to arrange this in hospital.
### Source boundary

This bundle is a 2025 reproduction of the clinician's working record. It is primary evidence of what Dr Monaghan supplied in 2025 and strong documentary evidence of the content of his retained working file. Where the repository already holds contemporaneous 2017 source pages, those earlier records remain the preferable source for proving the 2017 event itself.

The reproduced 2017 material records a plan to proceed cautiously with conventional dopaminergic therapy because of Liam's very young age and concern about dyskinesia and impulse-control complications. It also records that the case had been considered at a Neurology Complex Case meeting and that care with later levodopa/dopamine-agonist treatment had been advised with Prof Counihan and Neurology colleagues.

The same 2017 working record expressly raises a possible **PRKN / PARK2** explanation because of the very young onset, symmetry, akinetic-rigid presentation, lack of a dominant family history and preserved cognition. It records that PRKN/PARK2 testing or a broader panel was a reasonable option and refers to Prof Healy's interest in that possibility.
### Source boundary

The 2017 material establishes that PRKN/PARK2 was a contemporaneous diagnostic possibility, not that a PRKN diagnosis had been made. The later 2026 specialist genetic result is a separate evidential origin establishing the eventual genetic diagnosis.

The working file reproduces the 24 April 2018 Neurology record. It states that the Parkinson nurse had suggested stopping Procyclidine for approximately two weeks in Sept/Oct 2017 because of blurred vision and that, during that stop:
> “the first thing he noticed changing and changing rapidly was the return on the foot, of the outside left corn.”
The same passage records that symptoms worsened somewhat and that Liam was more **“shifty”** and **“unrelaxed”** off Procyclidine.
This is the same early treatment-response episode separately represented in the repository's 2018 Neurology source page and contemporaneous 24 October 2017 patient email.
The working file reproduces the 2020 Neurology material describing:
- a bad corn on the outside of the left foot;
- a left lower-limb “throw” with preserved dorsiflexion, plantarflexion, inversion and eversion power;
- the clinician's conclusion that this foot-throw appearance was parkinsonian rather than true foot drop;
- exquisite sensitivity of the feet;
- excessive movement and urge to move the feet.
These are later direct clinical observations and should not be treated as retrospective proof that every component of the 2017 foot syndrome was neurological.

The working file reproduces the October 2021 clinical record stating that ordinary Sinemet had first been introduced in September 2021 and increased as Kemadrin was withdrawn because of ocular-pressure/visual concerns.
The same record says Liam had been fully counselled and would receive a copy at home, followed by the categorical statement:
> “the DBS is only ever for the tremor element. It will not help with anything else.”
A narrower patient-specific clinical judgment may have been intended, but this bundle preserves the categorical wording actually recorded and supplied to the patient.

The opening complaint response states that Sinemet had been known to reduce Liam's experience of pain and that Dr Monaghan's own 10 March 2025 Sinemet CR prescription was **“also to try to help the morning experience including of pain.”**
It further records that the recent Sinemet CR escalation had provided **“profound relief currently.”**

The clinician's explanation remains that pain could have mixed or peripheral causes and that Parkinsonism/dopaminergic state could magnify the experience of pain; the response also preserves the stated rationale for cautious dose escalation in a young patient because of dyskinesia and dopamine-dysregulation/impulse-control risks.

Across the working file Dr Monaghan repeatedly states that his long clinic letters were intended to be copied to Liam and to create a shared understanding of what had been discussed, why decisions had been made and when.

This is evidence about the information framework the treating clinician says he deliberately supplied. It does not prove that Liam agreed with every proposition or that every discussion was fully understood in the same way by clinician and patient.

[Patient] was seen by our team and myself at Neurology Consults in AMU on Monday 2017 07 03rd.
I won't reiterate the whole story with a long narrative history because it is very much as per the summary above.
This is really quite long though, and this is in part because some of its purpose is for supply to [Patient].

This is an unusual situation and [Patient] has had a lot of questions most understandably and therefore this is also meant to consolidate a lot of discussions which we have had. Additionally it is in a way to help (as he termed himself) “with debriefing”; as well as to set out for him a clear plan for the gradual titration onto different treatment modalities.
We think that [Patient] unfortunately has a Parkinsonism.
Ordinarily, as you can imagine most individuals are diagnosed with idiopathic Parkinson – very effectively in the community by their General Practitioner and indeed often started on medications.

In the vast majority of cases our role is really to confirm and give the diagnosis and adjust the treatments. Generally this is achieved in a relatively short outpatient visit and we adjust the person’s medications and

just observe how things are. However for very obvious reasons given his very young age at the current time and moreover the possible very young age at onset maybe 13-14 years ago, I have been keen to keep [Patient] in Hospital until we could get an MRI scan.
I'm sorry for the delays in getting this done as an inpatient because obviously he was not prioritised by Radiology as this is a long-standing issue.

However in its own way, this has all suited us and [Patient] very well. It has allowed us get a lot done with [Patient] and explore a lot of questions in what is obviously a very challenging situation. He has learned a huge amount for the last week.

Moreover, the treatment options here are somewhat more limited than usual and not as dramatically effective for the person as might usually be the case where Levodopa/Dopamine Agonists may be introduced
This longer duration of an admission has helped us have a firmer footing going forward for having a plan of how things will be introduced.
Obviously I think it is particularly clear that he has an exceptionally high cognitive baseline and he has taken on things exceedingly well.

Moreover he is well able to say when he is being overwhelmed with too much information but he will carry-over excellently day-to-day and build on what he has learned, and question very appropriately with exceptional insight.

The question of how much information is too much is very valid. However again this is a circumstance of exceptional insight. While some of the documentation may be worrying to read, e.g. the risk of dementia in some form of Parkinson’s - - quite simply very quickly anyone could find this information on the internet and I want it to be clear that we are hopeful this will not be the case.
Parkinsons? – Typical / Atypical?
We think that the cause is a Parkinson's disease. However in many respects it is of course an atypical presentation:
###lack of prominent tremor.
###?13 years already i.e. very young age of onset
### symmetry is unusual – while he has asymmetry - to a degree, his movement disorder is more prominently symmetrical than assymetrical. This can be a feature of some genetic Parkinson’s
Form of Parkinsons/Parkinsonism?

In essence, most Parkinson's disease disorders are disorders of a protein called Synuclein or how Synuclein is handled - - whereas the Parkinson's plus disorders can be disorders of protein Synculein, or range of other protein disorders e.g. very prominently protein Tau.

It is an unpleasant analogy - and of course this is a very sensitive and deeply personal subject--- however an effective practical analogy which I have heard patients come up with themselves is perhaps the nature of: "rust" and rust “spreading”.

Any individual person can conceptulise that rust may be of different forms. While most people think of iron oxide as “rust” - - we all know that other forms of rust --- depending on the underlying metal --- can develop.

In a similar way, most Parkinson's disease protein abnormalities are of synculein whereas there are other forms of protein abnormalities in some parkinsonian disorders. Additionally in other conditions there are ways indeed that the same protein can present in different individuals - producing different disease forms (e.g. synuclein disorder also causes MSA and Lewy body disease – quite separately to more ordinary Parkinson’s disease).
Obviously there is a question of whether the previously used recreational drugs may have been a factor.

I suppose it is plausible. It is possible that recreational drugs used that may have been quite harmless in the rest of the population but may have accelerated the situation in [Patient] --- however I wouldn't have any great confidence in that explanation.

The larger question is whether the formulation and chemical composition of any of the agents previously used could have caused an MPTP like effect causing his Parkinsonsism. Again I am reluctant to accept that as an explanation either.
I suspect that this was always going to happen to [Patient] and I don’t want him having any idea that this was “caused”.

Himself [Patient] was worried that the alcohol was a factor? Aside from this being somewhat effective for him as a “de-tensioning” treatment over the years, and notwithstanding that 70 units of alcohol per week can have its own consequences and would not have been helping because of how alcohol can affect DNA repair mechanisms --- I really don't give much credence to the argument that the alcohol was any major factor in
this development of a Parkinsonian disorder in [Patient].
Genetics
I have explained to him the difficulties with the genetic assessment.
One of the chief difficulties with this is the question of whether a firm genetic diagnosis will actually actively change management?
This question is (in the majority of cases) usually answered in the negative.
In a way to explain genetics, I have in a very simplistic manner broken it up into 3 different concepts: -#1 what I term for [Patient]’s understanding as “strong genetics”

---where genetic disorders run very strongly through a family. We would terms these usually Autosomal Dominant.This is clearly not the case in [Patient]'s case and therefore it is not likely that these apply. It would not apply to most individuals with Parkinson's either. It is not a worry as he has no children as yet. #2 what I term for for [Patient]’s understanding as "moderate genetics"

---I use this example to explain where a person may have a range of different genes, many of them are currently unknown but which confer “susceptibilities” to Parkinson's. Depending on the combination of susceptibilities a person has genetically, then these, and various components of environment can contribute to the development of a Parkinson's disorder. This is a theory that probably applies to most people who actually develop Parkinson's disease “sporadically” or “idiopathically” who may have susceptibility genes that we do not understand the role of as yet or known genes with variations (e.g. in the LRRK2/ SNCA / GBA genes), as well as a range of possible environmental factors. #3---what I term for [Patient]’s understanding as "weak genetics"

---by this we mean the classical autosomal recessively inherited disorders that can occur within a family but which would be very unlikely to affect other family members. It is quite plausible that [Patient] may have one of these disorders as the cause for his Parkinsons/Parkinsonisms.

More specifically given a number of issues including his very young age of onset; the akinetic rigidity; the lack of a Dominant family history; and the marked symmetry; as well as how cognitively excellent [Patient] is, there is a question of whether the indicators are that he does have a PRKN gene disorder (PARK 2)?
Nervethless aspects may point to rarer monogenic explanations such as PARK 6 or PARK7 or even PARK 9 (the neuropathy question).
A summary of where we are with Genetics can be seen from this summary from the National Institutes of health in the US:
Genetic Testing in Parkinson's Disease

Genetic testing has recently become available for the parkin and PINK1 genes. Parkin is a large gene and testing is difficult. At the current stage of understanding, testing is likely to give a meaningful result only for people who develop the condition before the age of 30 years. PINK1 appears to be a rare cause of inherited Parkinson's disease. A small percentage (~2 percent) of those developing the condition at an early age appear to carry mutations in the PINK1 gene. Genetic testing for the PARK7, SNCA and LRRK2 genes is also available.

Individuals and families who are interested in having genetic testing can learn more about their risk for Parkinson's disease and the availability and accuracy of genetic testing for this disease by setting up an appointment with a genetics health professional. Genetic professionals work as members of health care teams providing information and support to individuals or families who have genetic disorders or may be at risk for inherited conditions. Genetic professionals can discuss the risks, benefits and limitations of available genetic testing for Parkinson's disease. See: Frequently Asked Questions about Genetic Counseling

Whatever form and whatever genetic cause is the cause, the question which is undoubtedly the most important is as regards therapy? Can we improve how the person is?

Ordinarily we would use levodopa or dopamine agonists however in these types of situations we tend to be extremely cautious in their usage for the reasons outlined in the summary on treatment and we will try to leave off on this for as long as possible.
No treatments are proven disease modifying, and all treatments are symptomatic – effective to varying degrees, and we will trying different symptomatic approaches with him first.
Treatment should be view in two ways:
1) Any disease modifying possibilities?
There is an unproven theoretical possible benefit giving him CoQ10 and this is started.
Azilect may be disease modifying by slowing whatever trajectory of progression a person is on.
2) Symptomatic therapy to improve his functioning and Quality of Life.

However Parkinson's is much more than simply a "movement disorder".
There are multiple other domains which can be affected and which in time may need considerable assistance, and these include urological function, bowel function, sleep function, and mood-affect.

Impression
This triceps is weak since the time of the onset of the pain. There was no obvious cause for this.

The problem is that triceps function is impaired . This could be a Radial nerve problem, or it could be in the posterior cord of the brachial plexus or more proximally in the roots / at the roots that subserve Triceps function - - for the radial: mainly C6,7,8.

It is fair to say (and he understands this actually quite accurately) that we certainly do not feel that the right arm-shoulder-triceps issue is anything to do primarily with his Parkinson’s disease. However it is the ordinary expectation that a person with Parkinson’s – they will have a more severe experience of pain than a person who would not have Parkinson’s has. Therefore I would imagine that this is quite painful disorder - but it is to be expected that his experience is worse.

In answer to his question, unfortunately, the somewhat improvement (limited) with the Neurontin gabapentin to does not give us indicators as to a likely cause. Whether it was the shoulder, or the brachial plexus, or the nerve roots, or something else completely different - any of these could potentially be improved by an anticonvulsant neurolytic drug for nerve pain - - because all pain is fundamentally mediated by nerves.

The triceps function is from the radial nerve predominantly C6-C7 and C8. However the radial nerve also has contributors from other nerve roots and therefore the element of pain and paraesthesia may not simply localise just to those defined levels.

That is why we do need to have the MRI to try to exclude any issues. This isn’t just C Spine and Shoulder – it is also brachial plexus – but while C Spine MRIs are easy to interpret, brachial Plexus and Shoulder MRIs are notoriously difficult. Negative MRIs don’t guarantee there isn’t a local issue. But a major problem is likely to be found. Conversely e.g. in a Brachial neuritis, an MRI might not show very much.
The actual cause for us is pretty important.
I genuinely do not know what the cause is here. As detailed above I did and do think it is nerve root problem because of how it is positionally exacerbated.
Nevertheless, I will very often be wrong in terms of that assessment. There are a range of other possibilities.
In a worse case scenario certainly there could be an infiltrating tumour of the lung apex but I think that is highly unlikely.

Additional causes could include brachial neuritis which just arises idiopathically for no reason-it is an inflammatory disorder of the brachial plexus (expected to arise as a post infectious disorder) or sometimes idiopathically as an autoimmune disorder i.e. for no reason we can define.

Also, it is reasonable that he could have pulled a muscle in the shoulder; torn a muscle or tendon or ligament, have an entrapment plexopathy, or caused some other irritative structural issue with the brachial plexus, or that he may even have a frozen shoulder notwithstanding the triceps extension problem which does seem to localise to nerve roots/or definably the proximal radial nerve.
Therefore in reality, there is a very very wide differential – and often an answer wont’ be found.

The major part of this is for [Patient] is about trying to make sure there is nothing truly major or serious and I think its fair to summaries that that is of major interest to him – to try to make sure there is nothing serious - -even if we can’t prove a cause.
Like many others, this may then be a case of trying to symptomatically manage this – as you have tried with the Neurontin.

We have not actually given IV steroids and indeed if [Patient] wanted we could do this. It would not be unreasonable to try if we are getting no where – even as a one off “test”. The problem with that approach or “test” is of course that as a general “dogma,” steroids will make “nearly anything better”. This is because of their potent anti-inflammatory abilities.

Things may or may not improve on them - but just because they would improve, does not necessarily give us a definable answer .F or example they could help in structural causes and they could help in compressive causes and they could help in inflammatory causes.

I had wondered about bringing [Patient] into Merlin Park and getting the MRI done there and indeed giving him a round of IV steroids over just three days as a short pulse which would be / should be safe - - we however we cannot do MRIs under general anaesthesia in Merlin Park.

A significant subset of people with Parkinson’s disease are going to get Parkinson’s disease dementia. I simply can’t guarantee this will not happen to him. He has significant worries and these are reasonable and appropriate worries. The age of onset he was at, was extremely young. It is simply absolutely and utterly impossible for us to predict with certainty his dementia risk. It would also be impossible to predict when he would get into trouble with dementia – IF EVER. The Kemadrin will never contribute to the development of a dementia state – in terms of “brain damage”.

Obviously the question becomes ---what can I do to reduce / limit my risk of dementia. There is no disease modifying therapies that we can offer.

The best evidence in terms of lifestyle measures for dementing illnesses obviously predominantly comes from Alzheimer’s disease. I think it is fair to say it is the generally held view that the lifestyle measures that would protect him against dementia are believed to have a significant impact, and are as follows:
A mixed varied diet with adequate fish/fish oils.
Novelty in life and engagement with new pursuits and activities.

Management of Depression/Anxiety , but there are not subjective features of either currently with [Patient], and not really other factors suggestive of that, other than this “irritability”.  Not smoking which is something that really does need to be addressed here.

The alcohol is now completely gone and that will be massively protective against this situation. I think it is fair to say that notions of “one drink per day being protective”, are not really accepted any longer. Even if there was any significant brian volume change on a current MRI we’d likely blame the alcohol as opposed to the iPD (Conversely other people can have excellent looking brains with iPD and still be very badly physically affected)

His own particular cognitive background both in terms of his intellect, and also his language based interests will be hugely neuroprotective. (the point is that he could have massive changes in brain volume over a long life and still actually score cognitively excellently on Neuropscyhological testing based on his Cognitive Reserve which without exaggeration or flattery, should be genuinely excellent)
As it happens I think it is necessary and wise to do the CT brain and the CT angiogram.

If he truly wishes to understand whether there are neurodegenerative brain volume changes already, it is an easy matter to ask for an MRI of the brain. This for example can be compared with his 2017 MRI and comment can be sought. We do not do volumetric assessments at the current time but they are a future scanning modality that will be available on an automated basis over the next decade (they are mainly at research stages now and they are not commonly done). However we can “eyeball it” and we can give him an answer if [Patient] requires it.

But it is an overly simplistic reduction to conceptulise dementing illnesses as purely a function of “brain volume”. It is actually about tract, connectivity and the loss of connections within the brain. While this can be reflected in brain volume, it is probably a poorer marker and in years to come we will probably use markers of connectivity and lack of connectivity as the real markers of dementia/predementia.
Incidentally if we did have particular neurocognitive dementing concerns about [Patient] right now, we might actually be doing a PET scan - - but I don’t think its necessary either.

First of all, it is an absolutely excellent result that the alcohol is completely gone.

**Source type:** primary institutional correspondence

Dear Mr. Moloney,

I have received communication arising from the Office of the Ombudsman in relation to apparent concerns which you have raised about the management of your complaint, which was first received by the Quality and Patient Safety Department on the 25th of March 2025.

I understand you have expressed concern with regard to the objectivity of the hospital’s approach to the management of your complaint. The purpose of my correspondence to you today is to provide you with additional clarity with regard to how complaints are managed.

The HSE Your Service Your Say (YSYS) Policy 2017 is underpinned by Part 9 of the 2004 Health Act and 2006 Complaints Regulations. This legislation exempts certain matters for examination under the YSYS policy. Section 48(1)(a) outlines that a person is not entitled to make a complaint about a matter relating solely to the exercise of clinical judgement by a person acting on behalf of the Executive (HSE).

As outlined in the letter of response issued on the 15th of April, a complaint that relates to matters of clinical judgment is always made available to the clinician whom the complaint is about, for their observations and response where appropriate. This is to afford the clinician an opportunity to respond to what has been alleged. Please note therefore that the role of a Complaints Officer in the case of matters of clinical judgment is not to investigate the matter, but to simply coordinate the management of the complaint. This involves ensuring that the complaint is received by the correct clinician, and that a response is provided back to the complainant. It is important to emphasise here that as matters of clinical judgement are exempt from examination under the YSYS policy, they are not subject to a Stage 3 and Stage 4 Review.

As you were not reassured by the response provided to you on 25th April, I consulted with the Clinical Director for Medicine in GUH, who agreed to have your complaint reviewed independently by the hospital’s incident management team to allay your concerns about transparency. You were advised of this in a letter issued to you on the 30th of May.
### YSYS
My role is to ensure a complaint that relates to a clinical issue is referred to the respective clinician who provided care, and to issue this response to the complainant in due course.
### Incident Management Framework (IMF)
Your complaint will be reviewed independently by an incident management team in accordance with this framework.
### Ongoing correspondence

I wish to thank you for your correspondence to date and the information which you have provided. Given the volume of correspondence received to date in relation to your complaint, and my commitment to a high volume of current open cases within my remit, I will require some time to review, collate and coordinate your complaint. In that regard, I ask that you kindly refrain from forwarding me any further correspondence and documentation at this time as this will only deter from advancing and progressing your complaint. I undertake to revert to you once the relevant personnel have reviewed your case and a response has been prepared.
I hope my correspondence has provided you with more clarity on the process and assurance that I play no part in the examination and further review of your complaint.
Yours sincerely,
Aoife Nolan
Quality & Patient Safety Coordinator and Complaints Officer
Quality and Patient Safety Department
Galway University Hospital

# Contemporaneous treatment-response emails — October 2017
Preserve contemporaneous patient-origin evidence about the effect of the neurological treatment regime before formal propositions are frozen.
This file distinguishes:
- what Liam wrote contemporaneously in October 2017;
- what Liam now recalls about the same episode;
- what can safely be inferred;
- what still requires the clinical record or expert interpretation.
**Source:** Gmail, sent by Liam Moloney to Celia Moloney, subject `Here`, 4 October 2017.

The email records Monaghan's staged Kemadrin/procyclidine titration and a planned treatment break to assess its effects. Liam wrote that within days of beginning half a tablet there had been significant improvement and described the period as `living in a miracle, literally`.
He listed concrete functional changes:
- `My walk is back together.`
- `My writing is good.`
- `I can stand up straight.`
- `My legs are loose and limber.`
- he could stand while the bus was moving;
- lift his bicycle without falling over it;
- jump, run, hop and skip;
- and perform ordinary dexterity tasks that had previously been difficult.
Four days into the Kemadrin break, he wrote:
> `I am feeling the tension building up, my feet are restless and my walk is falling apart....but my eyesight is back to normal.`

The same email also contains Liam's then-current historical reconstruction of the longstanding foot problem, including recurrent stinging on the outside of the left foot and years of severe burning foot pain. Importantly, it distinguishes foot pain from leg tension in his own experience while also trying to understand their place within the wider Parkinsonian illness.
### Source-status
This is contemporaneous patient evidence, written while the withdrawal experiment was actually occurring. It directly supports that:
- Kemadrin/procyclidine had produced marked global physical improvement;
- a planned withdrawal was being used to assess the medication's effects;
- during withdrawal, tension increased, the feet became restless and gait deteriorated;
- visual side effects were simultaneously improving off the medication.
It does **not**, by itself, prove the mechanism of the foot symptoms or that levodopa would have produced the same effect.
**Source:** Gmail, sent by Liam Moloney to Pauline McDonagh and Deborah Walsh, subject `Re: Medical Assessment`, 24 October 2017.

Liam told HR that he had had to stop the medication about three or four weeks earlier because it was affecting his eyesight; the Parkinson's nurse took him off it for about 12 days and reintroduced it at a lower dosage. He reported that the lower dose did not cover all symptoms and that the nurse had just advised increasing the dose again while monitoring vision.
The email records:
> `apart from the vision, I am physically very much improved, you wouldn't believe there was ever much wrong with me.`
and:
> `The joy of being able to move about normally and function unchallenged has been the equivalent of living in a miracle.`
At the same time Liam recorded that he had a Podiatry appointment on Thursday, Physiotherapy on Friday and the Parkinson's nurse on Monday.
### Source-status

This email corroborates, to a workplace recipient and for a practical occupational purpose, that the neurological medication regime had produced a profound physical improvement by October 2017, while visual toxicity was forcing withdrawal/reduction/re-escalation decisions.
It is particularly useful because it was not written for litigation, complaint or retrospective reconstruction.

Liam now clarifies that the improvement during procyclidine titration felt like a profound release of longstanding tension that had become almost a constant background `sound` in his bodily experience. He recalls being able to `walk with power` and experiencing the improvement as almost perfect apart from residual issues such as hand cramps and visual disturbance.

He further recalls that when procyclidine was withdrawn, the **first pain to return** was the focal pain on the outside of the left foot, the same pain he dates back to 2004, and that this focal pain persisted until March 2025.
### Source-status

The present recollection adds phenomenological detail not fully expressed in the surviving October emails. In particular, the claim that the outside-left-foot pain was the *first* symptom to return should remain tagged as present patient recollection unless and until a contemporaneous clinical note, email or witness source independently confirms that precise sequence.

The contemporaneous October emails do strongly support the broader state: dramatic improvement on Kemadrin/procyclidine, planned withdrawal to test effect, deterioration during withdrawal, foot restlessness during withdrawal, and re-escalation because the lower dose failed to control all symptoms.

objects.source_family: 4. Clinical significance to be tested, not assumed
objects.substantive_text: The clean documentary point is not that procyclidine proved the feet were dystonia and not that procyclidine and levodopa are interchangeable.

objects.source_family: 4. Clinical significance to be tested, not assumed
objects.substantive_text: It is narrower:

objects.source_family: 4. Clinical significance to be tested, not assumed
objects.substantive_text: > **Neurology's own treatment regime materially altered the patient's physical state, and the contemporaneous withdrawal experiment produced deterioration that included the feet.**

objects.source_family: 4. Clinical significance to be tested, not assumed
objects.substantive_text: Once that information existed, the neurological significance of treatment effects in the feet became a question requiring clinical interpretation.

objects.source_family: 4. Clinical significance to be tested, not assumed
objects.substantive_text: The later record should therefore be examined for whether Neurology documented what the medication-foot interaction meant, whether it changed the earlier Podiatry/Neurology allocation, and whether it entered the criteria governing prolonged dopaminergic deferral.
The GP record shows hospital diagnostic activity and formal communication to General Practice occurring at different times.
objects.title: GP communication and hospital activity were not simultaneous

objects.substantive_text: The controlled prescription facts show a December 2021 levodopa increase for dystonia/altered gait followed by an early January 2022 dose reduction without a stated reason in those prescription facts.
objects.title: The December 2021 / January 2022 dose reversal lacks a represented reasoning bridge

objects.substantive_text: The statement that the patient had a “good understanding” of why levodopa/dopamine agonists were being delayed is limited to that rationale and does not by itself establish agreement with every element of the wider case architecture.
objects.title: A narrow documented understanding should not be expanded into global agreement

objects.substantive_text: The integrated GP presentation, July uncertainty, Podiatry allocation, specialist PRKN reasoning, later treatment-state evidence and genetic confirmation can be established principally from GP, hospital, specialist, prescribing and genetic records.
objects.title: The central documentary chronology does not depend on later patient recollection

objects.substantive_text: A patient report recorded contemporaneously by a clinician should not be collapsed into the same source category as a later retrospective patient statement.
objects.title: Contemporaneously recorded patient report and later recollection are different evidential categories

objects.substantive_text: Local prescription or symptom-management changes can occur without an explicit rewriting of the historical classification; evidence of global reconsideration must be identified separately.
objects.title: Treatment change does not itself prove global diagnostic reconsideration

objects.substantive_text: The 2026 PRKN result establishes that the earlier PRKN etiological branch was real, but does not by itself identify the mechanism of every 2017 foot symptom.
objects.title: Later genetic confirmation validates the earlier PRKN branch without determining every historical symptom mechanism

objects.substantive_text: The full record contains both genuine structural/peripheral foot pathology and later Parkinsonian, dystonic, OFF-state and dopaminergic-response evidence; the documents alone do not justify reducing the longitudinal phenotype to either exclusive pole.
objects.title: The documentary record does not support an exclusively structural or exclusively neurological simplification

objects.documentary_tension: Before admission, the GP recorded bilateral foot pain with abnormal gait, later grouped the patient's “gait, feet and \"muscle tension\" issues” within the contemplated Neurology opinion, documented Occupational Health concern, increased bilateral leg tone and worsening dexterity, and arranged direct neurological assessment. During the neurological record, gait was described as footdrop-like and somewhat suggestive of dystonic posture, while the relationship between leg tension and the corns/callouses/foot pain was recorded as “Not clear”. The plan nevertheless separately routed the foot problem to outpatient Chiropody/Podiatry.
objects.possible_reconciliation: Structural pathology was genuinely present and could independently justify Podiatry involvement while Neurology continued to address tone, bradykinesia and gait. Parallel pathways need not imply a final etiological separation.
objects.title: Integrated pre-admission neurological concern vs later pathway separation
objects.what_would_resolve_it: The contemporaneous inpatient reasoning note, multidisciplinary discussion record, Podiatry referral text and subsequent Podiatry records identifying how the services understood the relationship.
objects.why_it_matters: The documents show a transition from an integrated referral problem to differentiated management pathways, but the presently represented facts do not themselves identify a definitive factual finding that resolved the foot component as neurologically separate before that routing occurred.

objects.documentary_tension: The neurological record expressly left the relationship between the leg symptoms and the corns/callouses/burning uncertain—“Not clear”—while the management plan contained a definite referral to outpatient Chiropody/Podiatry.
objects.possible_reconciliation: A service can appropriately treat a visible structural problem without deciding whether neurological posture, loading, peripheral pathology or another mechanism contributed to it.
objects.title: Express “Not clear” relationship vs definite Podiatry routing
objects.what_would_resolve_it: No further evidence is required to establish that the two documentary states coexisted; additional referral/pathway records would be needed to establish what conclusion, if any, Podiatry routing was intended to embody.
objects.why_it_matters: Clinical uncertainty and operational action can coexist, but the action alone cannot establish that the uncertainty had been resolved.

objects.documentary_tension: The GP recorded on 6 July 2017 that Podiatry would mark the case as priority “and as Parkinson's”. The neurological plan also separately requested outpatient Podiatry for the foot problem. The records therefore support both a Parkinson's-linked prioritisation label and a distinct Podiatry pathway.
objects.possible_reconciliation: “As Parkinson's” may have been a prioritisation or contextual label rather than a causal classification. Podiatry could still address structural foot disease in a patient with Parkinsonism.
objects.title: Podiatry priority “as Parkinson's” vs later use of a separate foot pathway
objects.what_would_resolve_it: The original Podiatry referral, telephone record and Podiatry triage/treatment notes.
objects.why_it_matters: The fact of Podiatry allocation cannot, without more, safely be used to prove that the foot problem had already been classified as independent of Parkinsonism.

objects.documentary_tension: The record documents marked mallet toes, onychogryphosis, callouses/pressure areas, pes planus and hammertoes, while also recording high tone and a footdrop-like gait somewhat suggestive of dystonic posture and expressly “NOT FOOT DROP”. The relationship between these domains was left “Not clear”.
objects.possible_reconciliation: Structural pathology, altered neurological posture/loading, pain amplification and separate peripheral mechanisms could have coexisted. The documentary record does not require one exclusive generator.
objects.title: Structural foot pathology vs neurological gait/posture findings
objects.what_would_resolve_it: Expert clinical evidence informed by the contemporaneous podiatric examination, neurological examination and any available foot imaging/pathway records.
objects.why_it_matters: Any later account that reduces the historical presentation to either a purely structural foot problem or a purely neurological foot problem would have to reconcile both sets of contemporaneous findings.

objects.documentary_tension: The record moved into Parkinson's/Parkinsonism coding and Long Term Illness administration while the clinical material still described an unusually young and atypical presentation and entertained autosomal-recessive/PARK2 explanations.
objects.possible_reconciliation: A Parkinson's/Parkinsonism diagnosis can be sufficiently established for treatment and administrative purposes while its genetic subtype remains unresolved.
objects.title: Atypical/genetic uncertainty vs administrative Parkinson's certainty
objects.what_would_resolve_it: No further evidence is required to show the distinction between syndrome-level diagnosis and etiological subtype; expert evidence would be needed only if a clinical consequence is said to follow from that distinction.
objects.why_it_matters: The administrative layer became definite at a time when the etiological/subtype layer remained open.

objects.documentary_tension: The records repeatedly state a preference to defer levodopa/dopamine-agonist therapy because of the patient's young age and treatment risks, while also recording that such therapy would sooner or later need to be considered, could make him “very much better”, and might produce a sustainable good response.
objects.possible_reconciliation: A clinician may reasonably acknowledge likely symptomatic benefit while deferring treatment because of anticipated long-term dyskinesia, impulse-control or tolerability concerns in a very young patient.
objects.title: Levodopa deferral vs acknowledged prospect of substantial benefit
objects.what_would_resolve_it: Contemporaneous notes setting out the trigger or threshold for treatment introduction, plus expert evidence on the clinical significance of the stated risks and benefits.
objects.why_it_matters: The documents articulate both the expected upside and the reasons for caution. The remaining question is what documentary threshold was intended to shift the balance from deferral to introduction.

objects.documentary_tension: The record repeatedly describes delaying ordinary dopaminergic therapy for as long as possible, later records that the patient felt undertreated, and then records introduction of a first levodopa drug in 2021. The presently represented facts do not identify a single documented rule explaining exactly what clinical state would reopen or end the deferral strategy.
objects.possible_reconciliation: The threshold may have been pragmatic and cumulative rather than a formal rule: worsening symptoms, intolerance of alternatives, patient preference and functional need may together have justified initiation.
objects.title: Persistent deferral strategy vs unidentified documentary reopening threshold
objects.what_would_resolve_it: The September/October 2021 decision note and any preceding movement-disorders nurse/consultant discussion documenting why the threshold was considered met.
objects.why_it_matters: The treatment transition is visible, but the documentary decision rule linking the earlier strategy to the later initiation is less explicit than the strategy itself.

objects.documentary_tension: Prof Healy recorded that the patient “probably has Park II” and suggested testing it initially. Galway records also identify PARK2/PRKN as a suspected cause, while explaining that testing could be deferred because it “doesn’t particularly change current management” and there was therefore “no great loss in ‘not knowing’ currently”.
objects.possible_reconciliation: Deferral can be rational where a genetic result is unlikely to change immediate symptomatic management and later testing may be technically broader or more informative.
objects.title: PRKN/PARK2 suspicion vs management-based reasons to defer genetic clarification
objects.what_would_resolve_it: Expert genetics/movement-disorders evidence on the clinical utility of testing at the relevant time and any contemporaneous discussion of non-management reasons for or against early confirmation.
objects.why_it_matters: Diagnostic information was expressly valued partly by whether it would alter current management, even though the suspected diagnosis was clinically specific and potentially relevant to prognosis and treatment sensitivity.

objects.documentary_tension: The GP recorded that the patient was doing well on Procyclidine; the specialist correspondence recorded a “dramatic improvement” in motor symptoms on low-dose Procyclidine with Rasagiline; and a planned treatment break was used to assess effects. The earlier relationship between leg tension and foot pathology had remained “Not clear”.
objects.possible_reconciliation: Procyclidine can alter motor tone or movement without proving the primary generator of corns, callouses or focal foot pain. Improvement in one domain does not establish a single mechanism for all foot symptoms.
objects.title: Procyclidine benefit vs unresolved lower-limb/foot classification
objects.what_would_resolve_it: Expert evidence on what can and cannot be inferred from the documented Procyclidine response, alongside contemporaneous symptom-by-symptom examination.
objects.why_it_matters: Medication-state evidence became available that was capable of bearing on tone, movement and function, while the original lower-limb/foot relationship remained unresolved.

objects.documentary_tension: During the planned Procyclidine break, the contemporaneous patient account recorded increasing tension, restless feet and a deteriorating walk. The later Neurology record stated that on stopping Procyclidine the first rapid change noticed was return of the outside-left-foot corn phenomenon, with worsening symptoms and feeling more “shifty” and “unrelaxed”. This sits alongside the earlier “Not clear” relationship between leg tension and foot pathology.
objects.possible_reconciliation: Medication withdrawal may change tone, movement, loading, restlessness or pain perception and thereby alter a structurally vulnerable foot without showing that the structural lesion itself was caused by Parkinsonism.
objects.title: Procyclidine withdrawal deterioration involving feet and gait vs earlier separation
objects.what_would_resolve_it: Expert interpretation of the pharmacological and biomechanical significance of the withdrawal/restart pattern and any contemporaneous clinical examination during the break.
objects.why_it_matters: The withdrawal episode supplied later evidence linking medication state, gait/tension and a foot phenomenon in time, without itself resolving mechanism.

objects.documentary_tension: In 2017 the record described a footdrop-like gait somewhat suggestive of dystonic posture but left the relationship between the leg symptoms and foot problems “Not clear”. In 2020, the clinician described a foot throw that looked a little like foot drop as “actually parkinsonian” because dorsiflexion, plantarflexion, inversion and eversion power were normal.
objects.possible_reconciliation: The 2020 “foot throw” may not have been identical to the 2017 structural pain/corn syndrome. A later Parkinsonian gait sign can coexist with independent structural foot disease.
objects.title: 2020 “actually parkinsonian” foot-throw assessment vs 2017 “Not clear” relationship
objects.what_would_resolve_it: Expert comparison of the 2017 and 2020 phenomenology, ideally with examination videos or contemporaneous gait documentation.
objects.why_it_matters: A later direct clinical interpretation assigns a Parkinsonian explanation to a lower-limb gait phenomenon that resembles a feature already observed in the earlier unresolved presentation.

objects.documentary_tension: By 2021 the patient was recorded as feeling undertreated, previous stiffness/aches were returning, increased Kemadrin was limited by visual intolerance, and Sinemet 50/12.5 mg BD was prescribed with the comment “↑ aches / pains / stiffness”. Earlier records had left the relationship between lower-limb tension and foot pathology unresolved.
objects.possible_reconciliation: “Aches / pains / stiffness” is broad language and does not establish that the prescription targeted the historical focal foot pathology. The treatment may have been directed at general Parkinsonian motor symptoms.
objects.title: 2021 Sinemet introduction for aches/pains/stiffness vs earlier lower-limb uncertainty
objects.what_would_resolve_it: The associated October 2021 clinical note or prescribing rationale identifying which symptoms were intended to be treated and how response was assessed.
objects.why_it_matters: Levodopa was eventually introduced in a treatment state explicitly involving aches, pains and stiffness, making later medication response potentially relevant to how lower-limb symptoms were conceptualised.

objects.documentary_tension: After Sinemet was introduced for increased aches, pains and stiffness and Kemadrin was stopped because of glaucoma/ocular-pressure concerns, the 22 December 2021 prescription stated that medication was being rationalised and levodopa slightly increased because of “re-emerging dystonia and altered gait”. The presently represented facts do not identify the intervening clinical examination that defined the re-emerging dystonia or connected it to specific body regions.
objects.possible_reconciliation: The phrase may reflect a contemporaneous clinical assessment documented elsewhere, including nurse review or direct observation that is simply absent from the current corpus.
objects.title: “Re-emerging dystonia and altered gait” rationale vs incomplete documentary bridge
objects.what_would_resolve_it: The clinical note, movement-disorders nurse record or assessment corresponding to the 22 December 2021 prescription.
objects.why_it_matters: The prescription provides a treatment rationale but not the full clinical reasoning bridge behind the terminology or phenotype being treated.

objects.documentary_tension: In 2023 the patient reported severe neuropathic pain in the feet, reduced mobility and shuffling, and being worse in the morning or later in the day if Sinemet had not been taken. The clinician assessed from the description that Parkinson's appeared undertreated and “the leg pain and shuffling is off related.” This later clinical reasoning sits alongside the 2017 possibility that leg/foot symptoms and corns/callouses/burning were separate or peripheral and “Not clear”.
objects.possible_reconciliation: The 2023 leg pain/shuffling may represent an OFF-related component superimposed on separate neuropathic or structural foot pain. Mixed mechanisms remain possible.
objects.title: 2023 OFF-related leg pain/shuffling assessment vs earlier peripheral/separate framing
objects.what_would_resolve_it: Expert comparison of symptom phenotype over time, together with contemporaneous examination during ON/OFF states and the underlying 2023 clinic record.
objects.why_it_matters: The later clinician assessment gives dopaminergic-state significance to leg pain and shuffling, potentially bearing on an earlier unresolved lower-limb relationship without automatically resolving the focal foot pathology.

objects.documentary_tension: After the patient reported worse symptoms when Sinemet had not been taken and the clinician assessed leg pain/shuffling as OFF-related, the plan was to trial morning Stalevo and see whether symptoms improved. The 28 September 2023 prescription implemented that morning substitution while continuing Sinemet for later doses.
objects.possible_reconciliation: The trial may have been directed primarily at shuffling and general OFF symptoms rather than at establishing the etiology of all foot pain.
objects.title: 2023 morning Stalevo substitution vs unresolved historical foot relationship
objects.what_would_resolve_it: The follow-up record documenting which symptoms changed after the morning substitution and how clinicians interpreted the response.
objects.why_it_matters: The record moved from symptom-state observation to a response-dependent medication change, which is capable of generating evidence relevant to the lower-limb phenotype.

objects.documentary_tension: The 10 March 2025 prescription instructed a response-dependent nighttime Sinemet CR trial. The later clinician response stated that the prescription was “also to try to help the morning experience including of pain” and that the recent escalation had provided “profound relief currently”. The same later explanation continued to allow mixed or peripheral causes and Parkinsonian amplification of pain.
objects.possible_reconciliation: Dopaminergic therapy may reduce an OFF-related, dystonic or pain-amplification component while structural or peripheral pathology remains present. Treatment response alone does not identify one exclusive cause.
objects.title: 2025 pain-targeted Sinemet CR and reported profound relief vs earlier mixed/peripheral framing
objects.what_would_resolve_it: Expert interpretation of the response and contemporaneous symptom mapping before and after Sinemet CR.
objects.why_it_matters: The later record expressly links dopaminergic treatment, morning pain and substantial reported relief while preserving a mixed-mechanism explanation rather than adopting a single causal account.

objects.documentary_tension: The 2017–2018 material identified PARK2/PRKN as a specific suspected cause and Prof Healy wrote that the patient probably had Park II. A later source described the treating team's belief and understanding as idiopathic Parkinson's disease. In 2026, genetic testing confirmed two pathogenic Parkin variants and Dr O'Riordan attributed the Parkinsonism and dystonia to compound heterozygous Parkin mutations.
objects.possible_reconciliation: “Idiopathic Parkinson's disease” may have been used as syndrome-level shorthand while the etiological subtype remained unconfirmed, rather than as a categorical denial of a genetic cause.
objects.title: Early PARK2/PRKN suspicion vs later idiopathic-PD representation vs genetic confirmation
objects.what_would_resolve_it: The context in which the later idiopathic terminology was used and expert clarification of whether it was intended etiologically or phenomenologically.
objects.why_it_matters: The later idiopathic-PD representation does not mirror the full earlier documentary uncertainty or the eventual genetic result.

objects.documentary_tension: The GP export records a hospital discharge date of 11 July 2017, while the DaTSCAN was completed on 13 July and an addendum/finalisation record thereafter incorporated the result. The discharge-summary message records final confirmation on 17 July at 19:30.
objects.possible_reconciliation: This is readily compatible with ordinary post-discharge test completion and later summary finalisation; the dates need not conflict.
objects.title: Physical discharge vs later DaTSCAN and documentary finalisation
objects.what_would_resolve_it: No further evidence is needed to reconcile the dates themselves. Transmission logs would be needed to establish exactly when each recipient received the later information.
objects.why_it_matters: The physical discharge date, diagnostic-result date and documentary-finalisation date are not the same event. Conclusions about what was known or communicated “at discharge” must therefore distinguish these stages.

objects.documentary_tension: The GP recorded on 14 July that Neurology had seen the patient but the GP was awaiting formal correspondence, and on 17 July recorded that no formal discharge had yet been received and that the patient was awaiting DaTSCAN results. The GP export later contains a discharge-summary message confirmed at 19:30 on 17 July, and by 18 July records extensive Monaghan correspondence, early Parkinsonism and a positive DaTSCAN.
objects.possible_reconciliation: Hospital findings may have existed before they were formally transmitted to or processed by the GP; the GP notes can therefore be accurate descriptions of information available at those particular moments.
objects.title: Hospital diagnostic activity vs GP receipt/knowledge chronology
objects.what_would_resolve_it: Electronic transmission/audit logs or message receipt timestamps for the discharge summary and Neurology correspondence.
objects.why_it_matters: The chronology distinguishes clinical events from the timing at which formal information reached or was entered into General Practice.

objects.documentary_tension: The contemporaneous record states that the patient had a good understanding of why levodopa or dopamine-agonist treatment was being delayed “at least for now”. Later material describes the long clinic letters more broadly as intended to create a shared understanding of what had been discussed, why decisions were made and when.
objects.possible_reconciliation: The later statement may describe the clinicians' communication objective rather than assert that the patient agreed with every clinical proposition.
objects.title: Narrow contemporaneous “good understanding” statement vs broader later shared-understanding representation
objects.what_would_resolve_it: Patient copies of the contemporaneous letters, consultation records and any direct contemporaneous documentation of questions, disagreement or agreement on specific issues.
objects.why_it_matters: The narrow contemporaneous statement supports understanding of the dopaminergic-delay rationale; it does not by itself establish agreement with, or understanding of, every aspect of the wider management architecture or unresolved foot classification.

objects.documentary_tension: On 22 December 2021, Stalevo was prescribed to rationalise medication and facilitate a small increase in levodopa because of “re-emerging dystonia and altered gait”, with alternative options described as limited by intolerance. On 4 January 2022, the prescribed Stalevo strength was reduced from 75/18.75/200 mg QDS to 50/12.5/200 mg QDS. The presently represented facts do not supply the clinical reasoning bridge for that reversal in dose direction.
objects.possible_reconciliation: The reduction may have followed side effects, tolerability, dyskinesia, patient preference or a clinical response documented elsewhere.
objects.title: December 2021 levodopa increase vs January 2022 reduction without a represented reasoning bridge
objects.what_would_resolve_it: The late-December/early-January clinical or nursing review corresponding to the prescription change.
objects.why_it_matters: The treatment state changed materially within a short interval, but the reason for the reduction is not represented in the fact set supporting these prescriptions.

objects.documentary_tension: Across several years, the record contains medication-state observations involving feet, gait, tension or pain: deterioration during Procyclidine withdrawal; later classification of a foot throw as “actually parkinsonian”; worse mobility and symptoms when Sinemet had not been taken; an OFF-related assessment of leg pain/shuffling; and later pain-targeted Sinemet CR followed by reported profound relief. At the same time, the later clinician explanation continues to preserve possible peripheral, structural and mixed causes.
objects.possible_reconciliation: The most coherent record-based reconciliation is a mixed phenotype: structural foot disease and/or peripheral pain could coexist with Parkinsonian dystonia, OFF-related movement changes and dopaminergic modulation of pain experience.
objects.title: Treatment-response evidence over time vs persistence of mixed-mechanism explanation
objects.what_would_resolve_it: Longitudinal expert review of the contemporaneous examinations, medication-response episodes and foot pathology, with symptom-specific rather than diagnosis-level analysis.
objects.why_it_matters: The cumulative later evidence is capable of bearing on the original uncertainty, but it does not by itself establish that every historical foot symptom shared one mechanism. The documentary question is how the accumulating treatment-state evidence was integrated with the continuing mixed-mechanism account.
